We identified 446 posts and analyzed over 6K comments to the posts that discussed security and privacy issues in almost all popular LIDEs, such as Cursor, Copilot, Codex, etc. Using a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods, we constructed a taxonomy of the reported security and privacy issues. Our results show that most issues in LIDEs stem from system-level design choices, rather than the underlying LLMs, such as user data access, unchecked autonomous actions, etc. To overcome these issues, developers frequently relied on external safeguards like code sandboxing and manual reviewing, highlighting prevalent mistrust among developers about LIDEs. We share lessons from our study to support future design of secure and privacy-aware LIDEs.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes security and privacy issues in LLM-native IDEs (LIDEs) by examining 1.1M Reddit posts, identifying 446 relevant posts and 6K+ comments. The study finds that most issues stem from system-level design choices (e.g., user data access, unchecked autonomous actions) rather than the LLMs themselves, and developers often rely on external safeguards due to mistrust.
AI.motivation: LIDEs have achieved significant success in SE tasks, but as software systems, they can exhibit vulnerabilities. The motivation is to systematically study the security and privacy issues developers encounter while using popular LIDEs, given the lack of comprehensive understanding of such issues in this emerging tool category.
AI.method: Collected 1.1M posts from 29 popular subreddits related to LIDEs; identified 446 posts and analyzed over 6K comments discussing security and privacy issues in LIDEs such as Cursor, Copilot, and Codex; used a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods to construct a taxonomy of reported issues.
AI.result: Most security and privacy issues in LIDEs arise from system-level design choices (e.g., user data access, unchecked autonomous actions) rather than the underlying LLMs. Developers frequently rely on external safeguards like code sandboxing and manual reviewing, indicating prevalent mistrust.
AI.conclusion: The study provides lessons to support the future design of secure and privacy-aware LIDEs, emphasizing the need to address system-level vulnerabilities beyond the LLM component itself.

title: Top-$k$ Pareto Bandits: Hypervolume Regret for Multi-Objective Slate Selection
summary: We consider a stochastic multi-objective bandit problem where, at each round, the agent selects a slate of $k$ arms and observes their $d$-dimensional reward vectors under semi-bandit feedback. We do not aim at identifying a single optimal arm; instead, we consider the problem of maintaining a small set of actions that jointly approximate the Pareto frontier. We formalize this objective through the dominated hypervolume induced by the selected subset of arms, and define an $α$-approximate hypervolume regret with respect to the best size-$k$ subset achievable in hindsight, where $α= 1 - 1/e$ reflects the approximation guarantee of greedy maximization for monotone submodular functions. To address this problem, we introduce \textit{THV-UCB}, an optimistic algorithm that selects arms greedily based on optimistic estimates of their marginal hypervolume contributions. We establish a gap-free regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{nkT})$ that holds on every instance, together with a gap-dependent bound $\tilde{O}(nk^{2.5}/Δ_{\min})$ that becomes polylogarithmic in $T$ once the arms are sufficiently well separated. Our results provide theoretical support for using small subsets to approximate Pareto fronts in various multi-objective applications.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a stochastic multi-objective bandit problem with semi-bandit feedback, where the goal is to select a slate of k arms to approximate the Pareto frontier. The authors introduce THV-UCB, an optimistic algorithm with greedy arm selection based on marginal hypervolume contributions, and provide both gap-free and gap-dependent regret bounds.
AI.motivation: In multi-objective bandits, existing work typically focuses on identifying a single optimal arm, but many real-world applications require maintaining a small set of actions that jointly approximate the Pareto frontier. The paper formalizes this problem using dominated hypervolume and defines α-approximate hypervolume regret.
AI.method: The proposed THV-UCB algorithm uses optimistic estimates of marginal hypervolume contributions to greedily select arms at each round. It leverages the submodularity of the hypervolume indicator to achieve an approximation guarantee of α = 1 - 1/e via greedy maximization.
AI.result: The paper proves a gap-free regret bound of Õ(d√(nkT)) that holds on every instance, and a gap-dependent bound of Õ(nk^{2.5}/Δ_min) that becomes polylogarithmic in T when arms are well-separated.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical results validate that using small subsets to approximate Pareto fronts is a viable approach in multi-objective bandit settings, offering provable regret guarantees.

title: CaM-Wolf: Causal-Aware Multimodal Agents for Social Deduction Games
summary: Social deduction games (SDGs) such as Werewolf have become challenging testbeds for AI agents. These games require complex social skills such as reasoning, deception, and collaboration. While recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have driven significant progress in SDG agents, current approaches are predominantly text-based, overlooking the multimodal nature that is fundamental to human social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce CaM-Wolf, the first SDG agent that integrates multimodal perception and generation. CaM-Wolf processes video inputs from other players, employs a causal-aware Reasoner trained via reinforcement learning to establish logical chains between observable behaviors and hidden roles, and presents itself through an animated avatar. Our experiments and user study show that CaM-Wolf achieves superior agent gameplay performance and enhances the quality of human-AI interaction. This work represents a significant advancement towards creating more human-like AI agents capable of participating in nuanced social dynamics. Our code is available at https://3dagentworld.github.io/avatar_wolf.

AI.tldr: CaM-Wolf is the first social deduction game agent that integrates multimodal perception (video input) and generation (animated avatars), using a causal-aware Reasoner trained via reinforcement learning to bridge behavioral observations and hidden roles, achieving superior gameplay and human-AI interaction quality.
AI.motivation: Current SDG agents are predominantly text-based and overlook the multimodal nature fundamental to human social interaction; this paper aims to bridge that gap by introducing multimodal perception and generation capabilities.
AI.method: Integrates video input processing from other players, employs a causal-aware Reasoner trained via reinforcement learning to establish logical chains between observable behaviors and hidden roles, and presents itself through an animated avatar.
AI.result: Superior agent gameplay performance and enhanced quality of human-AI interaction, as demonstrated by experiments and user study.
AI.conclusion: This work represents a significant advancement towards creating more human-like AI agents capable of participating in nuanced social dynamics.

title: BG-REAL: A Public Real-Data Anchored Benchmark for Background Manipulation Detection and Localization
summary: Background manipulation is a practical but under-specified image-forensics setting: the manipulated evidence can sit outside the salient foreground object, while many evaluations emphasize object-centric copy-move, splicing, or generic synthetic edits. We introduce BG-REAL, a public real-data anchored benchmark package for background manipulation detection and localization. The current release is built from Open Images V7 instance-segmentation sources and contains 7,000 processed samples over 1,200 source groups, including 6,000 public-data anchored samples and 1,000 synthetic control samples. BG-REAL covers six edit families, matched authentic controls, source-group splits, mask and leakage QA, 599 human-assisted quality-control rows, three completed external baselines (TruFor, MVSS-Net, and HiFi-Net), and five-seed model evaluation. Beyond aggregate accuracy, we use matched-authentic-control diagnostics to measure how often baselines misclassify re-encoded authentic images as manipulated at a threshold fixed on held-out validation data; false-positive rates range from 0.57 (TruFor, the lowest) to 1.00 (several weak or mask-informed baselines), indicating that re-encoding artifacts are a shared shortcut risk across baselines rather than a problem specific to any one model. The release provides the construction pipeline, evaluation protocol, paper-ready figures, and reproduction documentation. We frame BG-REAL as a background-manipulation-focused complement to general image-manipulation-localization benchmarks, not as a fully real-only or general-purpose benchmark.

AI.tldr: BG-REAL is a public benchmark package for background manipulation detection and localization, built from Open Images V7 with 7,000 samples across six edit families, including 599 human-verified rows and three baseline evaluations. Key finding: re-encoding artifacts cause high false-positive rates (0.57–1.00) across all tested baselines, revealing a shared shortcut risk.
AI.motivation: Background manipulation is a practical but under-specified forensics setting where manipulated evidence often lies outside salient foreground objects, yet existing benchmarks emphasize object-centric manipulations (copy-move, splicing, generic synthetic edits).
AI.method: Constructed from Open Images V7 instance-segmentation sources; contains 7,000 processed samples over 1,200 source groups (6,000 public-data anchored + 1,000 synthetic controls); covers six edit families with matched authentic controls, source-group splits, mask/leakage QA, and 599 human-assisted QC rows. Evaluates three baselines (TruFor, MVSS-Net, HiFi-Net) with five-seed model evaluation using matched-authentic-control diagnostics.
AI.result: False-positive rates range from 0.57 (TruFor, lowest) to 1.00 (several weak/mask-informed baselines) when classifying re-encoded authentic images as manipulated at a fixed threshold, indicating re-encoding artifacts are a shared shortcut risk across all baselines.
AI.conclusion: BG-REAL is a background-manipulation-focused complement to general image-manipulation-localization benchmarks, not a fully real-only or general-purpose benchmark. Provides construction pipeline, evaluation protocol, paper-ready figures, and reproduction documentation.

title: ExplainBench: Evaluating Code Explanations from Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have seen rapid adoption in software engineering. As agents take a greater role in the actual generation of code, they are making larger changes, spanning tens to hundreds of lines. This makes manual review of agent results increasingly infeasible, leading developers to turn to explanations to understand enacted changes. Despite this, there are no benchmarks that evaluate the trustworthiness of agent-generated explanations. To bridge this gap, we propose ExplainBench, a benchmark to automatically evaluate explanations from coding agents. ExplainBench is based on the intuition that informative explanations should enable an LLM to correctly answer questions, allowing quantitative comparison of explanation quality between agents. With this observation, we construct a suite of questions that evaluates whether explanations accurately describe (1) the intended behavior of buggy code and (2) the effect of applying the agent patch itself. Experiments first reveal that explanation quality is a distinct axis of agent evaluation: ExplainBench ranks agents differently from the widely-used SWE-bench Verified benchmark. A deeper breakdown of explanation quality in agents shows frequent problems in explanations, such that explanations often claim that a patch is correct when it is not. Based on this insight, we implement and evaluate an explanation audit agent which runs additional tests to validate and refine explanations. This agent improved the explanations of all evaluated agents, demonstrating agent explanations can be automatically made more trustworthy.

AI.tldr: Proposes ExplainBench, a benchmark to automatically evaluate the trustworthiness of explanations from LLM coding agents, revealing that explanation quality is a distinct evaluation axis from code correctness and that agent explanations often claim incorrect patches are correct.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents generate increasingly large code changes (tens to hundreds of lines), manual review becomes infeasible, yet there are no benchmarks to evaluate the trustworthiness of agent-generated explanations about the changes they make.
AI.method: ExplainBench evaluates explanation quality by testing whether explanations enable an LLM to correctly answer questions about (1) the intended behavior of buggy code and (2) the effect of applying the agent's patch. The benchmark also introduces an explanation audit agent that runs additional tests to validate and refine explanations.
AI.result: ExplainBench ranks agents differently from SWE-bench Verified, showing explanation quality is a distinct evaluation dimension. Explanations frequently claim incorrect patches are correct. The audit agent improves explanations across all evaluated agents.
AI.conclusion: Agent explanation quality is a distinct and important axis for evaluation, and explanations can be automatically made more trustworthy through audit mechanisms.

title: FloDR: An invertible dimensionality reduction method based on a normalising flow
summary: It is common for two-dimensional embeddings of high-dimensional data to be read far beyond what they can support. Distances in and between clusters, the meaning behind empty spaces, and the amount of structure hidden at each point are generally invisible in the output of methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. This is because the information that could support the meaning of these properties is discarded during the optimisation process. Here, we present FloDR, a dimensionality reduction method that embeds data through an invertible normalising flow. While FloDR only uses the first two output coordinates to create a two-dimensional embedding, it retains the remaining coordinates rather than discarding them. In addition to the embedding, an exact inverse and an exact density are properties of a trained mapping, which enable diagnostic visualisations that are computed from the exact inverse of the model that drew the layout rather than from an approximate one. Specifically, we draw two fields, the conditional spread, which measures how much of the original data remains undetermined at each embedding position in input units, and the hidden contrast, which measures how much information about a labelled contrast the two plotted coordinates discard. Both fields are rendered with a prespecified test against a held out portion of the input data and a bootstrap confidence. A field that fails the test is reported as refused.

AI.tldr: FloDR is an invertible normalizing flow-based dimensionality reduction method that retains all coordinates (not just the first two) to enable exact inverse mapping and density estimation, allowing diagnostic visualizations like conditional spread and hidden contrast with statistical testing.
AI.motivation: Standard 2D embeddings (t-SNE, UMAP) discard high-dimensional information during optimization, making distances, cluster structures, and hidden patterns uninterpretable; there is no way to know what information is lost or if the embedding is trustworthy.
AI.method: FloDR uses normalizing flows to learn an invertible mapping from high-dimensional data to a latent space; it plots only the first two coordinates for visualization but retains all other coordinates to preserve full information; diagnostic visualizations (conditional spread, hidden contrast) are computed from the exact inverse and density, tested against held-out data with bootstrap confidence.
AI.result: The method produces exact inverse mappings and exact densities as properties of the trained model; diagnostic fields (conditional spread, hidden contrast) are rendered with statistical tests against held-out data; fields failing the test are reported as refused.
AI.conclusion: FloDR enables trustworthy 2D embeddings by providing exact diagnostics (not approximations) that reveal where the embedding is reliable, how much information is discarded, and what structure remains hidden.

title: Spline-Based Boundary Representations for Sparse View Reconstruction and Simulation Using Isogeometric Analysis
summary: Image-based reconstruction aims to recover three-dimensional geometry from images. Recent advances have enabled the recovery of visually detailed models, yet their representations are not well-suited for numerical simulation. Simulation frameworks typically require explicit, watertight, and smooth geometries to ensure numerical robustness and accuracy, properties that surfaces extracted from image-based reconstructions lack. We propose FORGE-SIM, a method to directly reconstruct a multi-patch B-spline boundary representation from sparse posed RGB images without manual intervention. By optimizing the spline representation itself, our approach produces compact, smooth, and watertight geometries that are natively compatible with both Computer Aided Design and simulation workflows. Additionally, we introduce a strategy to project observation-derived fields, such as a thermal state and semantic information, onto the reconstructed models in the same spline basis, enabling immediate use in simulation. We demonstrate that the obtained models are of sufficiently high quality to enable thermal simulation and modal analysis. By unifying image-based reconstruction and simulation-ready modeling within a single optimization framework, this work removes a long-standing barrier between computer vision and numerical analysis. We anticipate that it will enable new workflows for simulation-driven design, inspection, and digital twin applications.

AI.tldr: FORGE-SIM directly reconstructs multi-patch B-spline boundary representations from sparse posed RGB images, producing compact, smooth, watertight geometries compatible with CAD and simulation workflows, and enables projection of observation-derived fields (e.g., thermal, semantic) for immediate simulation use.
AI.motivation: Image-based reconstructions produce visually detailed models but lack watertight, smooth geometries needed for numerical simulation. This gap prevents direct use of reconstructed models in simulation-driven applications.
AI.method: Optimizes a multi-patch B-spline boundary representation directly from sparse posed RGB images within a single optimization framework, and projects observation-derived fields (thermal, semantic) onto the same spline basis.
AI.result: Produces compact, smooth, watertight geometries natively compatible with CAD and simulation; demonstrated successful thermal simulation and modal analysis.
AI.conclusion: Bridges computer vision and numerical analysis by unifying image-based reconstruction and simulation-ready modeling, enabling new workflows for simulation-driven design, inspection, and digital twins.

title: MultiFixer: A Coordinator-Proposer Based Multi-Agent Framework For Fixing Multi-Hunk Bugs
comment: Accepted to 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: Automated Program Repair (APR) has benefited greatly from Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing LLM-based APR methods still struggle with multi-hunk bugs that require coordinated changes across multiple locations. These bugs demand repository-level context understanding, repair-order scheduling, and effective hunk-level patch generation and selection. To address these challenges, we propose MultiFixer, a novel Coordinator-Proposer based multi-agent framework for multi-hunk repair. MultiFixer performs tool-augmented bug analysis, constructs fine-grained repair context, iteratively generates patches through a Coordinator-Proposer architecture, and applies two-stage patch refinement for syntactic and semantic correctness. We evaluate MultiFixer on 835 bugs from Defects4J and three vulnerability benchmarks. On Defects4J, MultiFixer fixes 326 bugs, including 62 multi-method and 27 multi-file bugs, and outperforms prior APR baselines in the reported comparisons with the same base model. Moreover, MultiFixer also fixes 46 multi-hunk bugs among 95 unique fixes. When combined with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, MultiFixer repairs 420 bugs, establishing a new state of the art on Defects4J. On VUL4J, MultiFixer repairs 24 real-world vulnerabilities, including 5 multi-hunk cases. On the multi-hunk subsets of SEC-bench and PatchEval, MultiFixer fixes 11 and 19 vulnerabilities, respectively, outperforming all compared baselines under GPT-3.5. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MultiFixer for multi-hunk repair.

AI.tldr: MultiFixer is a novel Coordinator-Proposer based multi-agent framework for multi-hunk program repair that fixes 326 bugs on Defects4J, including 62 multi-method and 27 multi-file bugs, establishing a new state of the art when combined with Claude-3.5-Sonnet (420 fixes).
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based APR methods struggle with multi-hunk bugs requiring coordinated changes across multiple locations, as they demand repository-level context understanding, repair-order scheduling, and effective hunk-level patch generation and selection.
AI.method: MultiFixer employs a Coordinator-Proposer multi-agent framework with tool-augmented bug analysis, fine-grained repair context construction, iterative patch generation, and two-stage patch refinement for syntactic and semantic correctness.
AI.result: On Defects4J, MultiFixer fixes 326 bugs (62 multi-method, 27 multi-file, 46 multi-hunk), outperforming prior APR baselines. Combined with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, it repairs 420 bugs (new SOTA). On VUL4J: 24 fixes (5 multi-hunk). On SEC-bench and PatchEval multi-hunk subsets: 11 and 19 fixes respectively, outperforming baselines under GPT-3.5.
AI.conclusion: MultiFixer effectively addresses multi-hunk repair challenges through its multi-agent architecture and refinement pipeline, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.

title: Entity Resolution in Practice: Lessons from a Self-Serve Pipeline
summary: We built and evaluated a self-serve entity resolution (ER) system on six benchmarks spanning 864 to 5M records, and three lessons emerged that are absent from existing ER literature. (1) No single matching algorithm wins everywhere - a self-serve pipeline cannot predict its next dataset, so we recommend training several algorithm families per dataset and letting an automatic bake-off pick the winner. (2) Precision and recall need separate fixes, not a shared threshold - precision needs hard rule-based vetoes, recall needs more diverse candidate retrieval. (3) One false-positive link can silently merge unrelated entities - assuming "A matches B" and "B matches C" implies "A matches C" lets a single bad link chain hundreds of records together, so every cross-group merge must be actively re-verified. We hope these lessons save practitioners the months of dead-end experiments that led us to them.

AI.tldr: A self-serve entity resolution system was built and evaluated across six benchmarks, revealing three key lessons: (1) no single algorithm works universally, so multiple algorithm families should be trained per dataset with an automatic bake-off to select the best; (2) precision and recall require separate fixes (rule-based vetoes for precision, diverse candidate retrieval for recall) rather than a shared threshold; (3) transitive closure of matches (A≈B & B≈C ⇒ A≈C) is dangerous because a single false positive can chain-merge unrelated entities, so every cross-group merge must be actively re-verified.
AI.motivation: Existing ER literature lacks guidance on building practical, self-serve systems that work across diverse, unseen datasets without manual tuning. The authors aimed to distill generalizable lessons from building such a system.
AI.method: Built and evaluated a self-serve ER pipeline on six benchmarks (864 to 5M records). Tested multiple algorithm families and compared performance via an automatic bake-off to select the best configuration per dataset.
AI.result: Found that no single algorithm dominates; different datasets require different algorithms. Precision and recall respond to different levers (hard vetoes vs. diverse retrieval). Transitive merging propagates errors catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: Recommendations for self-serve ER: use multi-algorithm bake-offs, decouple precision/recall fixes, and avoid transitive closure without active re-verification of cross-group merges.

title: MultivationBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Sequential Motivation Reasoning
comment: 31 pages, including appendices; 6 figures and 22 tables. Code: https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/MultivationBench
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have sparked significant interest due to their potential for social intelligence; however, their ability to perform sequential motivation reasoning remains insufficiently studied. Existing evaluations predominantly examine static text or isolated visual snapshots, which do not reflect the cumulative nature of real-world behavioral drivers. To address this gap, we introduce MultivationBench, a benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate multimodal motivation reasoning within story-driven visual narratives. The benchmark builds upon established psychological frameworks - Maslow's hierarchy and Reiss's basic desires - and requires models to integrate accumulated multimodal context to infer evolving motivations. Results indicate that MultivationBench presents a significant challenge: all tested models struggle to maintain consistent motivation reasoning across sequential contexts, revealing a critical disconnect between static recognition capabilities and the dynamic reasoning essential for human-like social understanding.

AI.tldr: MultivationBench is a new benchmark evaluating multimodal LLMs' ability to reason about evolving motivations across sequential visual narratives, revealing that current models struggle with dynamic motivation inference despite performing well on static tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of multimodal LLMs focus on static text or isolated visual snapshots, failing to assess sequential motivation reasoning that reflects real-world behavioral drivers.
AI.method: The benchmark builds on Maslow's hierarchy and Reiss's basic desires, requiring models to integrate accumulated multimodal context across story-driven visual narratives to infer evolving motivations.
AI.result: All tested models struggle to maintain consistent motivation reasoning across sequential contexts, revealing a critical disconnect between static recognition and dynamic reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal LLMs lack the dynamic, context-integrative reasoning needed for human-like social understanding, highlighting a key gap for future model development.

title: LumaGuide: Distribution Shaping for Training-Free HDR Generation in Diffusion Models
summary: Pretrained diffusion models generate realistic images but are constrained by the statistical biases of their training data, limiting their ability to produce high dynamic range (HDR) content. In this work, we introduce LumaGuide, a training-free framework for distribution shaping in diffusion models. Instead of modifying model parameters, LumaGuide steers the sampling process to match target feature distributions via differentiable energy-based guidance. We instantiate this framework for HDR generation by controlling luminance distributions in perceptually uniform PQ space. Our results show that aligning luminance histograms is sufficient to induce HDR-consistent behavior, including coherent highlights and preserved shadow detail, while maintaining semantic fidelity. Beyond HDR, LumaGuide enables flexible specification of target distributions through data-driven presets, reference images, or text-driven predictors, and extends naturally to video generation with temporal consistency constraints. More broadly, our work demonstrates that controllable generation can be achieved by directly shaping output distributions at sampling time, without retraining diffusion models.

AI.tldr: LumaGuide is a training-free framework that shapes output distributions of pretrained diffusion models during sampling, enabling HDR image generation by controlling luminance histograms in PQ space, without retraining. It extends to video and supports flexible distribution control via presets, references, or text.
AI.motivation: Pretrained diffusion models are limited by training data biases and cannot produce high dynamic range (HDR) content. The authors aim to enable HDR generation without retraining by directly shaping the output distribution at sampling time.
AI.method: Training-free framework using differentiable energy-based guidance to steer the diffusion sampling process toward target feature distributions. Specifically instantiated for HDR by aligning luminance histograms in perceptually uniform PQ space.
AI.result: Aligning luminance histograms induces HDR-consistent behavior: coherent highlights, preserved shadow detail, and maintained semantic fidelity. The approach supports data-driven presets, reference images, text-driven predictors, and extends to video with temporal consistency.
AI.conclusion: Controllable generation can be achieved by directly shaping output distributions at sampling time without retraining diffusion models, demonstrating a general paradigm for distribution shaping in generative models.

title: Tangling Pull Requests: Curating a Commit Untangling Dataset from Merged PRs
summary:
Composite commits (CC), in which multiple unrelated changes are bundled into a single commit, are frequent in software development and significantly hinder code comprehension and maintenance. Although machine learning-based methods have been developed to ``untangle'' such commits into smaller, coherent change sets, these methods require large-scale training data with correct untangling labels. Preparing such datasets is costly and typically requires expert labelling.
  In this study, we propose a scalable and cost-effective method for dataset construction by leveraging commits extracted from open-source repositories' pull requests (PRs). We empirically validated our dataset and found that when applying our filtering rules, PRs that, when viewed as a single commit, are tangled, yet each individual commit on the feature branch is atomic (ideal PRs), increased from 9.5% to 55%. This composite commits dataset is more than 5.7 times larger than previous heuristic-based datasets.
  Using our new dataset, we find that the PR-based dataset differs statistically from previous datasets directly constructed using Herzig's proposed heuristics even after accounting for our proposed rules that may alter CC or STS sizes. When constructing datasets using the previous heuristics, they differ statistically along dimensions that impact the confidence voters and are likely to impact learning-based approaches. We validate the impact on the original Herzig \etal method, which used confidence voters across our dataset.
  To show that our approach extends to other languages, we also create a Python dataset which we empirically validate, finding comparable rates for ideal PRs (56.5%).

AI.tldr: This paper presents a scalable method for constructing composite commit datasets by leveraging pull requests from open-source repositories, achieving 55% ideal PRs (up from 9.5%) and creating a dataset 5.7x larger than prior heuristic-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing ML-based commit untangling methods require large-scale, high-quality labeled datasets that are costly to produce, as they typically require expert annotation.
AI.method: The authors propose leveraging pull requests (PRs) from open-source repositories: PRs where the overall merge is tangled but individual commits on the feature branch are atomic (ideal PRs). They apply filtering rules to increase the proportion of such ideal PRs from 9.5% to 55%.
AI.result: The resulting CC dataset is 5.7x larger than previous heuristic-based datasets. The PR-based dataset differs statistically from prior heuristic-based datasets (e.g., Herzig et al.) across dimensions affecting confidence voters. The approach also extends to Python with comparable ideal PR rates (56.5%).
AI.conclusion: The proposed PR-based method is a scalable, cost-effective alternative for constructing composite commit datasets, improving data quality and size for training machine learning-based commit untangling methods.

title: Learning Implicit Causal World Models from Multi-Agent Demonstrations
summary: In model-based reinforcement learning, world models exist as internal simulators, but their training often conflates statistical correlations with causal mechanisms. This problem is exacerbated in multi-agent systems where physical transitions are intertwined with strategic agent intents, causing world models to fail under distribution shift. We introduce Implicit Causal World Models to recover environmental dynamics from offline demonstrations without requiring pre-defined causal graphs. By incorporating policy variance, we render world models discoverable via the sequential backdoor condition. Evaluations across coordination tasks (Two-Door, Navigation, and Giveway) demonstrate that these models provide interpretable causal representations under both full and partial observability, with model accuracy scaling directly with interventional strength.

AI.tldr: Implicit Causal World Models (ICWM) recover causal environmental dynamics from offline multi-agent demonstrations without pre-defined causal graphs, using policy variance and sequential backdoor adjustment to disentangle physical transitions from agent intents, achieving interpretable representations that scale with interventional strength under full/partial observability.
AI.motivation: World models in model-based RL conflate statistical correlations with causal mechanisms, especially in multi-agent systems where physical transitions and strategic agent intents are intertwined, causing failure under distribution shift.
AI.method: Introduce Implicit Causal World Models (ICWMs) that recover environmental dynamics from offline demonstrations without requiring pre-defined causal graphs, using policy variance to render world models discoverable via the sequential backdoor condition.
AI.result: Evaluated on coordination tasks (Two-Door, Navigation, Giveway), the models provide interpretable causal representations under both full and partial observability, with model accuracy scaling directly with interventional strength.
AI.conclusion: ICWMs effectively disentangle causal mechanisms from correlations in multi-agent dynamics, enabling robust world models that scale with interventional strength and provide interpretable representations.

title: EvoPINN: Agentic Discovery of Executable Algorithms for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet their performance heavily relies on the manual, trial-and-error engineering of neural representations, loss formulations, and optimization dynamics. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for automated design, unconstrained code generation often yields mathematically invalid or numerically unstable solutions under strict scientific computing constraints. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{EvoPINN}, an agentic framework that reformulates PINN development from labor-intensive manual design into a rigorous, execution-grounded algorithm discovery problem. EvoPINN navigates a modular search space by decoupling neural representations from training programs, utilizing an LLM agent to iteratively propose memory-conditioned programmatic modifications. To ensure scientific validity, all candidates undergo strict structural verification and budget-matched PDE evaluation. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE regimes (oscillatory, elliptic, dissipative, and nonlinear transport) demonstrate that EvoPINN discovers PDE-specialized learning algorithms that significantly reduce relative $L_{2}$ error compared to baselines. Crucially, EvoPINN autonomously invented SLRC-PINN, a novel architecture whose performance gains persist under rigorous parameter-matched comparisons, establishing the viability of execution-grounded agents for discovering genuinely new scientific computing mechanisms.

AI.tldr: EvoPINN is an LLM-agentic framework that automates the design of physics-informed neural networks by treating PINN development as an execution-grounded algorithm discovery problem, using iterative programmatic modifications with structural verification and budget-matched PDE evaluation.
AI.motivation: PINN performance depends on manual, trial-and-error engineering of neural representations, loss formulations, and optimization dynamics. LLM-based unconstrained code generation often produces mathematically invalid or numerically unstable solutions under strict scientific computing constraints.
AI.method: EvoPINN decouples neural representations from training programs in a modular search space, uses an LLM agent to iteratively propose memory-conditioned programmatic modifications, applies strict structural verification and budget-matched PDE evaluation to ensure scientific validity.
AI.result: EvoPINN discovers PDE-specialized learning algorithms that significantly reduce relative L2 error across oscillatory, elliptic, dissipative, and nonlinear transport PDE regimes. It autonomously invented SLRC-PINN, a novel architecture with persistent performance gains under parameter-matched comparisons.
AI.conclusion: EvoPINN establishes the viability of execution-grounded LLM agents for discovering genuinely new scientific computing mechanisms, moving PINN development from manual design to automated algorithm discovery.

title: Lightweight Image Classification of Raptor Species for Edge Devices: Rare-Species Dataset Expansion via Video Frame Extraction, Knowledge Distillation, and TensorRT Deployment
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. English translation of a paper submitted to IPSJ (in Japanese); the Japanese version is the source of record
summary: We investigate lightweight raptor-species classification for real-time edge deployment in wind-turbine collision mitigation. Using DINOv2-L (304M parameters) as a teacher, we distilled three lightweight students (MobileNetV4, ViT-Small, and EfficientNet-B0). To reduce confusion between closely related species, we expanded the dataset to 12,519 images, including an increase in Steller's Sea Eagle images from 463 to 2,050 via video-frame extraction. Under a group split that separates samples at the video- and source-image level to mitigate source leakage at that granularity, the three-student ensemble achieved a macro recall of 0.935 +/- 0.004 over five distillation seeds (0.955 on a conventional image-level split, retaining 97.5% of the teacher's macro recall) with roughly one-eighth as many parameters. On a subset of 1,258 images disjoint from the former training images, White-tailed Eagle recall improved by up to 38.6 percentage points, while the rate at which it was misclassified as the Steller's Sea Eagle decreased from 61% to 15% of errors. TensorRT FP16 deployment of EfficientNet-B0 on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano achieved 3.19 ms/image including host-device transfer (313 images/s), with 99.95% argmax agreement with FP32. In five-seed controlled comparisons, neither distillation (versus CE-only) nor the change from a DINOv2-L to a DINOv3-L teacher yielded a clear ensemble-level improvement; the primary gains stem from the dataset expansion and teacher re-fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: A lightweight raptor classification system for wind-turbine collision mitigation uses knowledge distillation (DINOv2-L teacher → MobileNetV4, ViT-Small, EfficientNet-B0 students). Dataset expansion to 12,519 images (especially Steller's Sea Eagle via video-frame extraction) with group split to prevent data leakage yields a three-student ensemble achieving macro recall 0.935±0.004 (group split) and 0.955 (image split), retaining 97.5% teacher performance with ~1/8 parameters. TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano achieves 313 images/s (3.19 ms/image). Gains primarily come from dataset expansion and teacher fine-tuning, not distillation or teacher choice.
AI.motivation: To enable real-time edge deployment of accurate raptor species classification for wind-turbine collision mitigation systems, addressing challenges of closely related species confusion (especially White-tailed vs. Steller's Sea Eagle) and computational constraints of edge hardware.
AI.method: Knowledge distillation from DINOv2-L (304M params) to three lightweight students (MobileNetV4, ViT-Small, EfficientNet-B0); dataset expansion to 12,519 images with video-frame extraction for Steller's Sea Eagle (463→2,050); group split at video/source-image level to prevent source leakage; TensorRT FP16 deployment optimization on Jetson Orin Nano; controlled comparisons across five seeds for distillation and teacher variants.
AI.result: Three-student ensemble: macro recall 0.935±0.004 (group split), 0.955 (image split), 97.5% of teacher performance with ~1/8 parameters. White-tailed Eagle recall improved up to 38.6 pp; misclassification as Steller's Sea Eagle dropped from 61%→15% of errors. TensorRT FP16: 3.19 ms/image (313 images/s), 99.95% argmax agreement with FP32. No clear ensemble-level improvement from distillation or DINOv3-L teacher change.
AI.conclusion: Primary performance gains stem from dataset expansion and teacher re-fine-tuning rather than distillation technique or teacher model choice. Lightweight students are feasible for real-time edge deployment in raptor collision mitigation.

title: CodeSpec: Dual Executable Specifications for Agentic Long-Horizon Feature Development
summary: LLM-based code agents have advanced repository-level software development through iterative interaction with codebases and tools. However, feature development requires integrating new behaviors into existing architectures through coherent cross-component functional chains. Existing agents typically derive such chains through free-form reasoning, often producing unreliable feature designs with incomplete functional chains. Moreover, textual designs are difficult to verify and enforce, making it challenging to maintain design-implementation consistency throughout long-horizon development. We propose CodeSpec, a dual executable specification method for repository-level feature development. It builds reliable functional chains from evidence pairing sub-requirement semantics with repository architectures, then compiles them into complementary architecture and behavior specifications that check chain completeness and correctness while preserving design-implementation consistency over long interactions. On FeatureBench, which targets feature development in existing repositories, CodeSpec achieves 70.7%, 55.0%, and 49.9% pass rates under DeepSeek-V4-Pro, outperforming representative baselines such as Claude Code. Results on the repository generation benchmark NL2Repo-Bench further demonstrate its generalizability.

AI.tldr: CodeSpec proposes a dual executable specification method for repository-level feature development that builds reliable functional chains from evidence pairing sub-requirement semantics with repository architectures, and compiles them into complementary architecture and behavior specifications to ensure design-implementation consistency, achieving 70.7%, 55.0%, and 49.9% pass rates on FeatureBench with DeepSeek-V4-Pro.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based code agents use free-form reasoning to derive functional chains for feature development, which often produces unreliable feature designs with incomplete functional chains, and textual designs are difficult to verify and enforce, making design-implementation consistency challenging over long-horizon development.
AI.method: CodeSpec employs a dual executable specification approach: it builds reliable functional chains by pairing sub-requirement semantics with repository architectures as evidence, then compiles these chains into complementary architecture and behavior specifications that check chain completeness and correctness while preserving design-implementation consistency over long interactions.
AI.result: On FeatureBench, CodeSpec achieves 70.7%, 55.0%, and 49.9% pass rates under DeepSeek-V4-Pro, outperforming representative baselines like Claude Code. Results on NL2Repo-Bench further demonstrate its generalizability.
AI.conclusion: CodeSpec effectively improves reliability and consistency in repository-level feature development by using dual executable specifications to guide functional chain construction and maintain design-implementation alignment, outperforming existing code agents.

title: RAGuard: A Layered Defense Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems Against Data Poisoning
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS ResponsibleFM 2025, AAAI FrontierIR 2026
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) in external corpora, but this reliance exposes them to corpus poisoning: maliciously injected passages that manipulate retrieved evidence. We introduce RAGuard, a layered defense against \emph{factual} corpus-poisoning attacks on RAG pipelines. The first layer adversarially fine-tunes a dense retriever on synthetic poisoned documents (fabricated facts, contradictions, and reasoning traps), teaching it to downrank malicious passages before generation. The second layer, the Zero-Knowledge Inference Patch ZKIP, is a label-free, black-box filter: for each retrieved document, it performs a leave-one-out decode and scores the document by the semantic shift and output-entropy change that its removal induces. ZKIP requires no poison labels, no ground-truth answers, and no access to model internals; it compares the model's own answers under counterfactual contexts. On poisoned Natural Questions at 5--30\% poison ratios, adversarial retriever training alone reduces but does not eliminate attack success, while ZKIP drives the measured attack success rate to 0.000 in every defended configuration, keeping Recall@5 within 0.03 of the clean-corpus baseline. Supervised analyses on both Natural Questions and BEIR (NFCorpus) confirm that the counterfactual signals ZKIP relies on carry learnable poison structure. The defense costs $k{+}1$ generator passes per query ($6\times$ for $k{=}5$); we analyze batching and early-stopping approximations that reduce this overhead. We also show that keyword-preserving poisons leave lexical retrievers such as BM25 essentially unaffected, an observation that delineates the boundary of the threat model. Code, datasets, and evaluation harnesses are released for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: RAGuard is a two-layer defense (adversarial retriever fine-tuning + ZKIP filter) against factual corpus-poisoning attacks in RAG systems, achieving 0% attack success rate with minimal recall degradation.
AI.motivation: RAG systems ground LLMs in external corpora, making them vulnerable to corpus poisoning—malicious passages that manipulate retrieved evidence. Existing defenses are insufficient, motivating a layered approach against factual poisoning.
AI.method: Two-layer defense: (1) Adversarial fine-tuning of a dense retriever on synthetic poisoned documents, and (2) Zero-Knowledge Inference Patch (ZKIP)—a label-free, black-box filter that performs leave-one-out decoding and scores documents by semantic shift and output-entropy change when removed.
AI.result: On poisoned Natural Questions (5-30% poison ratios), adversarial retriever training reduces but does not eliminate attack success; ZKIP drives attack success rate to 0.000 in all defended configurations, with Recall@5 within 0.03 of clean baseline.
AI.conclusion: RAGuard provides robust defense against factual corpus poisoning with minimal retrieval degradation. ZKIP's counterfactual signals carry learnable poison structure. The defense incurs k+1 generator passes per query, with batching/early-stopping approximations available. Keyword-preserving poisons leave lexical retrievers unaffected, delineating threat model boundaries.

title: Evidence-Ledger Adjudication for Claim-Evidence Traceability
summary: AI agents can draft claims faster than authors can check whether the cited or retrieved evidence supports them. We study evidence-ledger adjudication: a claim-evidence traceability workflow that pairs each claim with an evidence packet, assigns a support relation, and routes unsupported, contradicted, or mixed-evidence claims back to the author. The empirical core is a 2,335-row blind benchmark built from independent external labels in AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact. Gold relations and source evidence labels are hidden during prediction and joined only for scoring. On this benchmark, the agent evidence-ledger condition achieves 0.676 relation accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1, compared with 0.383 accuracy and 0.303 macro-F1 for the best non-agent baseline. It also routes 1270/1435 claims whose gold labels indicate contradiction, missing evidence, or mixed evidence, while routing 295/900 supported claims. These results show that evidence-ledger adjudication can turn heterogeneous evidence packets into an auditable traceability layer for AI-assisted writing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces evidence-ledger adjudication, a workflow that pairs AI-drafted claims with evidence packets, assigns support relations, and routes problematic claims back to authors. A 2,335-row blind benchmark shows the agent achieves 0.676 accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1, significantly outperforming baselines, and correctly routes 88.5% of unsupported/contradicted claims while flagging only 32.8% of supported ones.
AI.motivation: AI agents generate claims faster than authors can verify whether cited or retrieved evidence actually supports them, creating a critical bottleneck in trustworthiness and accountability for AI-assisted writing.
AI.method: The authors propose evidence-ledger adjudication: a traceability workflow that pairs each claim with an evidence packet, assigns a support relation (supported, unsupported, contradicted, mixed), and routes unsupported/contradicted/mixed-evidence claims back to the author. They build a 2,233-row blind benchmark from AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact, hiding gold relations and source evidence labels during prediction.
AI.result: The agent evidence-ledger condition achieves 0.676 relation accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1 versus 0.383 accuracy and 0.303 macro-F1 for the best non-agent baseline. It routes 1,270/1,435 claims with gold labels of contradiction, missing, or mixed evidence, while routing 295/900 supported claims.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-ledger adjudication can transform heterogeneous evidence packets into an auditable traceability layer for AI-assisted writing, significantly improving claim-evidence verification and routing of problematic content.

title: Comparing the Performance of Foundation Model Derived Embeddings with Traditional Approaches for Distant Metastasis Prediction in Head and Neck Cancer
comment: 27 pages including supplemental materials, 5 main figures, 2 supplemental figures, 5 main tables, 7 supplemental tables. Poster Abstract at 2026 AAPM Meeting and Exhibition
summary: Background: Early prediction of distant metastasis (DM) risk in head and neck cancer (HNC) can enable timely interventions that may improve treatment outcomes. Many current machine learning methods rely on prior knowledge of the region of interest such as tumor segmentations, which require expert knowledge, is time-consuming and introduces user-dependent variability. Medical image-based foundation models have recently been developed for specific imaging modalities to streamline down-stream prediction tasks by extracting modality-relevant features. Purpose: In this study, we evaluate the effectiveness of using a foundation model as the feature extractor to predict DM risk in HNC patients and compare its performance with traditional approaches that require prior knowledge on the regions of interest. Methods: Preoperative CT images of 2327 patients from the RADCURE dataset were used. Three features-sets were created including radiomics, deep-learning based features, and CT Foundation derived features. The feature-sets were used individually in a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to predict DM risk. Results: The model using CT Foundation embeddings outperformed the radiomics and deep learning-based models, achieving a Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.791, compared to AUC values of 0.772 and 0.753 for the radiomics and deep learning-based models, respectively. The CT Foundation based model had similar performance to a model that combined the use of radiomics and deep learning-based features that achieved an AUC of 0.794. Conclusions: Features based on foundation models offer a promising alternative to traditional radiomics while reducing the need for domain expertise and extensively annotated datasets. Their minimal preprocessing requirements also make them a more accessible and scalable option.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates using a CT-based foundation model as a feature extractor to predict distant metastasis risk in head and neck cancer patients. The CT Foundation embeddings achieved an AUC of 0.791, outperforming radiomics (0.772) and deep learning (0.753) models, while matching the combined radiomics+deep learning model (0.794), without requiring tumor segmentations or domain expertise.
AI.motivation: Early prediction of distant metastasis (DM) risk in head and neck cancer (HNC) can improve treatment outcomes. Current machine learning methods require prior knowledge like tumor segmentations, which are time-consuming, require expert knowledge, and introduce user-dependent variability. Foundation models trained on specific imaging modalities may streamline prediction by extracting modality-relevant features without such manual input.
AI.method: Preoperative CT images of 2,327 HNC patients from the RADCURE dataset were used. Three feature sets were created: radiomics features, deep learning-based features, and CT Foundation-derived features. Each feature set was fed into a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to predict DM risk. Model performance was evaluated using AUC.
AI.result: The CT Foundation-based model achieved an AUC of 0.791, outperforming the radiomics model (0.772) and the deep learning-based model (0.753). Its performance was comparable to a combined radiomics + deep learning model (AUC of 0.794).
AI.conclusion: Features from foundation models are a promising alternative to traditional radiomics, reducing the need for domain expertise and extensive annotations. Their minimal preprocessing requirements make them more accessible and scalable for DM risk prediction in HNC.

title: MRCoder: An Efficient Context Selecting Approach for Repository-Level Code Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation. However, repository-level code generation remains challenging, as it requires effectively identifying and utilizing repository-specific context. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporates relevant code snippets, it often introduces redundant context that interferes with the LLM's ability to utilize relevant information, leading to degraded generation quality and increased computational cost. Moreover, existing context selection and compression methods struggle to balance efficiency and quality, either introducing additional computational overhead or failing to effectively select valid context. In this paper, we propose MRCoder, an efficient context selection framework that improves both the effectiveness and efficiency of repository-level code generation. MRCoder adopts a Map-Reduce paradigm: in the Map Phase, a lightweight draft model generates drafts over partitioned contexts, and Structure-Aware Draft-Guided Selection (SADGS) selects informative contexts based on drafts through API consistency and logical similarity; in the Reduce Phase, the refined contexts are aggregated for final generation, with a parallel verification strategy further accelerating decoding. We evaluate MRCoder on two widely used repository-level code generation benchmarks, CoderEval and DevEval, using Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder as backbone LLMs. Experimental results show that MRCoder improves code generation accuracy over strong baselines while reducing token consumption by 30 to 50% and inference time by up to 52%. These results demonstrate that our proposed structured and draft-guided context selection strategy is crucial for improving both the quality and efficiency of repository-level code generation

AI.tldr: MRCoder is a Map-Reduce-based context selection framework for repository-level code generation that uses a lightweight draft model to select informative contexts via Structure-Aware Draft-Guided Selection (SADGS), improving generation accuracy while reducing token consumption by 30-50% and inference time by up to 52%.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches for repository-level code generation often introduce redundant context that degrades generation quality and increases computational cost, while current context selection and compression methods struggle to balance efficiency and quality.
AI.method: MRCoder employs a Map-Reduce paradigm: (1) Map Phase uses a lightweight draft model to generate drafts over partitioned contexts, then applies Structure-Aware Draft-Guided Selection (SADGS) to select informative contexts based on API consistency and logical similarity; (2) Reduce Phase aggregates refined contexts for final generation with parallel verification for decoding acceleration.
AI.result: On CoderEval and DevEval benchmarks using Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder backbones, MRCoder improves code generation accuracy over strong baselines while reducing token consumption by 30-50% and inference time by up to 52%.
AI.conclusion: Structured and draft-guided context selection is crucial for improving both the quality and efficiency of repository-level code generation.

title: Automorphism-Induced Non-Canonicity in Top-k Explanations of Graph Neural Networks
summary: A gradient-based GNN explainer given a molecule with two chemically equivalent nitro groups assigns them attribution scores that are equal to the last bit. It cannot do otherwise: message passing is exactly permutation equivariant, so any automorphism of the input leaves every attribution invariant. Yet the standard report, the top-k edges, names one of the two, and which one is settled by the order of an array. We show this is a structural obstruction rather than an implementation slip. When no minimal valid explanation is fixed by the input's automorphism group, no rule can be single-valued, minimal and symmetry-respecting at once. For the exact-k reports used in practice we give a parameter-free criterion, mechanised in Lean 4 with no axiom dependencies, that decides from the graph alone whether every score-optimal report of that size must split an orbit. Across 21298 instance-budget decisions the criterion agrees with a mechanical model-equivalence check without exception, and no severing case we found admitted a neutral alternative. The obstruction is common. Nontrivial automorphisms occur in 93.4% of Mutagenicity, the dataset the seminal explainability papers use, so the measure-zero dismissal of symmetric inputs, sound on the continuous domains it was made for, collapses here. At the sparsity budget those papers report, 24.0% of molecules with two interchangeable nitro groups (6 of 25) surface exactly one of them, every one arbitrary under mechanical verification. A model's blindness also manufactures symmetry: every MUTAG molecule contains atoms chemistry separates and the network provably cannot, and a matched control shows the resolution is set by what the model reads rather than how it is parameterised. Reporting orbits removes the arbitrariness at 0.11 ms and 0.43 extra edges per graph.

AI.tldr: GNN explainers produce arbitrary explanations for symmetric inputs due to permutation equivariance, and we provide a formal criterion and practical solution.
AI.motivation: Current GNN explainers assign arbitrary explanations when the input has automorphisms (e.g., chemically equivalent nitro groups), yet this arbitrariness has been dismissed as a measure-zero issue from continuous domains.
AI.method: We formalize the obstruction: when no minimal valid explanation is fixed by the input's automorphism group, no rule can be single-valued, minimal, and symmetry-respecting. We provide a parameter-free criterion (mechanised in Lean 4) that decides from the graph alone whether every score-optimal report must split an orbit. Validate against 21,298 instance-budget decisions and a mechanical model-equivalence check.
AI.result: The criterion agrees with model-equivalence checks without exception. Nontrivial automorphisms occur in 93.4% of Mutagenicity; 24.0% of molecules with two interchangeable nitro groups surface exactly one (arbitrarily). Reporting orbits removes arbitrariness at 0.11 ms and 0.43 extra edges per graph.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-induced arbitrariness in GNN explanations is pervasive, not a negligible edge case, and reporting orbits is an efficient, principled remedy.

title: Eco3S: Complex Socio-Economic System Simulation via Agent-Based Models
summary: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has renewed interest in agent-based modeling (ABM). However, current LLM-based ABM research faces several key challenges: modeling evolving agent-environment interactions, enabling flexible counterfactual reasoning, and automating simulation workflows for scientific research. In this paper, we propose Eco3S, a socio-economic system simulation framework for economic research and policy analysis that addresses these challenges through three key mechanisms: (1) Co-evolving Environment Design, a bidirectional feedback loop where agents and the environment co-evolve, producing realistic emergent behaviors; (2) Structural Causal Simulation, a structural causal model (SCM)-inspired counterfactual mechanism that allows flexible interventions for diverse causal inference tasks; (3) Simulation-Analysis-Refinement Paradigm, a self-corrective mechanism that iteratively refines experimental designs based on prior simulation results. Experiments on diverse economic scenarios confirm \textit{Eco3S}'s effectiveness in replicating multiple established economic studies (canal decay, origins of governance, and information propagation) and phenomena across domains. Additional results further demonstrate its scalability and generalizability, highlighting the framework's potential for rigorous economic research and policy-making.

AI.tldr: Eco3S is a socio-economic simulation framework for LLM-based agent-based modeling that addresses evolving agent-environment interactions, counterfactual reasoning, and automated simulation workflows through co-evolving environment design, structural causal simulation, and a self-corrective refinement paradigm.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based ABM research faces challenges in modeling evolving agent-environment interactions, enabling flexible counterfactual reasoning, and automating simulation workflows for scientific research.
AI.method: Eco3S proposes three mechanisms: (1) Co-evolving Environment Design with bidirectional feedback loops; (2) Structural Causal Simulation inspired by SCM for counterfactual interventions; (3) Simulation-Analysis-Refinement Paradigm for iterative self-correction of experimental designs.
AI.result: Eco3S effectively replicates multiple established economic studies (canal decay, origins of governance, information propagation) and shows scalability and generalizability across diverse economic scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Eco3S demonstrates strong potential for rigorous economic research and policy-making by enabling realistic emergent behaviors, flexible causal inference, and automated refinement of simulations.

title: HeteroPROPMT: A Real-time and Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception Framework
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). 9 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables
summary: Collaborative Perception (CP) improves autonomous systems' awareness of their surroundings by sharing sensor data, intermediate features, and detection results. In real-world deployments, however, collaborating vehicles often use heterogeneous sensors, perception models, datasets, and training domains, creating feature-space shifts that degrade downstream fusion and detection. Existing approaches typically retrain fusion and detection components or introduce modality-specific feature interpreters. These methods scale poorly to newly joining agents and often require access to proprietary metadata, raising privacy concerns. We propose HeteroPROMPT, a real-time and privacy-preserving framework for heterogeneous collaborative perception. HeteroPROMPT rapidly aligns each heterogeneous agent's features with an ego-centric unified feature space through modular prompts and lightweight learning-based tuning, while keeping agent encoders and the collaborative fusion and detection stacks frozen. Its visual prompt-based training and inference modulate Bird's Eye View (BEV) features across channels and spatial locations with low computational overhead. For metadata-free deployment, an autoencoder learns a compact unified representation and extracts modality cues from shared features, enabling real-time modality classification and routing to the appropriate HeteroPROMPT modules without exposing proprietary agent information. Experiments on the OPV2V-H and V2XSet datasets show that HeteroPROMPT improves Average Precision over state-of-the-art heterogeneous CP methods while using orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters. This offers a scalable and practical CP solution. The proposed modality classifier also predicts the joining agent's modality from compact features with greater than 99.99 percent accuracy during deployment. Code will be available at https://github.com/arminmaleki007/HeteroPROMPT.

AI.tldr: HeteroPROMPT is a real-time, privacy-preserving framework that aligns heterogeneous agent features into a unified BEV space using lightweight visual prompts and an autoencoder for modality classification, achieving state-of-the-art detection performance with minimal trainable parameters and no need for proprietary metadata.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous collaborative perception methods require retraining fusion/detection components or accessing proprietary metadata, which scales poorly to new agents and raises privacy concerns. A lightweight, privacy-preserving solution is needed.
AI.method: HeteroPROMPT uses modular visual prompts to modulate BEV features across channels and spatial locations, keeping agent encoders and fusion/detection stacks frozen. An autoencoder learns a compact unified representation and extracts modality cues from shared features for real-time modality routing without exposing proprietary information.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art heterogeneous CP methods on OPV2V-H and V2XSet datasets while using orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters. Modality classifier achieves >99.99% accuracy on joining agent's modality from compact features.
AI.conclusion: HeteroPROMPT offers a scalable, privacy-preserving, and real-time solution for heterogeneous collaborative perception, enabling rapid onboarding of new agents without retraining or metadata exposure.

title: A First Look at Coding Agents' Compliance with AI Contribution Rules in Open-Source Communities
summary: Open source communities have been flooded with AI-generated contributions. In defense, they have written contribution rules to regulate coding agents' behavior, spanning from a total ban, mandatory disclosure, to verification gates and human sign-offs. Yet, whether coding agents read and follow those rules, and behave in open source repositories, remains unknown. To estimate real-world rule compliance of coding agents, we curate 106 issues from 49 repositories containing AI contribution rules into RepoComplianceBench. We judge the trajectory of each run against the repository's rules, measuring whether the agent refuses to contribute, discloses its assistance truthfully, clears the required verification gates, or escalates critical steps to a human. We also test if extra prompts, rule disclosure, or feedback from the compliance verifier help with the situation. Our experiments on four frontier models show that today's agents almost never proactively retrieve the contribution rules. Agents pick up disclosure and verification with reminder prompts, rule quotes, and verifier feedback; however, they never refuse to contribute in AI-banned repositories under any condition we tested. The status reveals that verification and disclosure issues are solvable with existing mechanisms, yet enforcing bans and human escalations remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RepoComplianceBench, a benchmark of 106 issues from 49 repositories with AI contribution rules, to evaluate whether coding agents comply with these rules (ban, disclosure, verification, human sign-offs). Testing four frontier models shows agents rarely proactively retrieve rules, can learn disclosure/verification with prompts but never refuse to contribute in banned repositories, revealing that bans and human escalations remain unsolved.
AI.motivation: Open source communities are flooded with AI-generated contributions and have created contribution rules to regulate coding agents, but it's unknown whether agents actually read and follow these rules in real-world repositories.
AI.method: Curated 106 issues from 49 repositories with AI contribution rules into RepoComplianceBench, judged agent trajectories against repository rules across four dimensions (refusal, disclosure, verification, human escalation), and tested extra prompts, rule disclosure, and verifier feedback interventions.
AI.result: Frontier models almost never proactively retrieve contribution rules; they can learn disclosure and verification with reminders/quotes/feedback, but never refuse to contribute in AI-banned repositories under any tested condition.
AI.conclusion: Verification and disclosure issues are solvable with existing mechanisms, but enforcing bans and human escalation remains an open problem.

title: MetaKoopman: Bayesian Meta-Learning of Koopman Operators for Modeling Structured Dynamics under Distribution Shifts
summary: Modeling and forecasting nonlinear dynamics under distribution shifts is essential for robust decision-making in real-world systems. In this work, we propose MetaKoopman, a Bayesian meta-learning framework for modeling nonlinear dynamics through linear latent representations. MetaKoopman learns a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart (MNIW) prior over the Koopman operator, enabling closed-form Bayesian updates conditioned on recent trajectory segments. Moreover, it provides a closed-form posterior predictive distribution over future state trajectories, capturing both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in the learned dynamics. We evaluate MetaKoopman on a full-scale autonomous truck and trailer system across a wide range of adverse winter scenarios, including snow, ice, and mixed-friction conditions, as well as in simulated control tasks with diverse distribution shifts. MetaKoopman consistently outperforms prior approaches in multi-step prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to distributional shifts. Field experiments further demonstrate its effectiveness in dynamically feasible motion planning, particularly during evasive maneuvers and operation at the limits of traction. Project website: https://mahmoud-selim.github.io/MetaKoopman/

AI.tldr: MetaKoopman is a Bayesian meta-learning framework that models nonlinear dynamics under distribution shifts via linear latent Koopman representations, using a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart prior for closed-form Bayesian updates and predictive distributions. It outperforms prior methods in prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness, validated on autonomous truck-trailer systems in adverse winter conditions and simulated control tasks.
AI.motivation: Modeling and forecasting nonlinear dynamics under distribution shifts is critical for robust decision-making in real-world systems, but existing approaches struggle with uncertainty quantification and adaptability to changing conditions.
AI.method: MetaKoopman learns a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart (MNIW) prior over the Koopman operator, enabling closed-form Bayesian updates conditioned on trajectory segments and providing a closed-form posterior predictive distribution that captures both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms prior approaches in multi-step prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to distributional shifts. Validated on full-scale autonomous truck-trailer systems in snow, ice, and mixed-friction conditions, as well as simulated control tasks.
AI.conclusion: MetaKoopman enables effective dynamically feasible motion planning under distribution shifts, particularly during evasive maneuvers and operation at traction limits, demonstrating practical utility in real-world field experiments.

title: Fewer Clarifications, Better Code: Benchmarking Cross-Session Personalized Ambiguity Adaptation in Coding Assistants
summary: AI-assisted coding increasingly translates informal user intent into executable software, yet coding requests often contain ambiguities that recur in user-specific ways across tasks and sessions. Existing disambiguation methods typically address each ambiguous request in isolation within the current coding session, often through eliciting additional clarification. However, whether resolved session history from the same user can serve as memory for resolving recurring personalized ambiguity in a newly opened session remains underexplored. We formulate personalized ambiguity adaptation as a new task: given a user's previously resolved coding sessions and a new ambiguous request, an assistant should identify the recurring ambiguity pattern, produce the intended executable solution, and minimize clarification. To benchmark this task, we introduce CAPA, which characterizes personalized coding ambiguity through six mechanisms and injects these mechanisms into unambiguous executable tasks using a controlled three-stage generation pipeline. CAPA contains 600 coding sessions across 60 balanced user--ambiguity cells, including 300 held-out evaluation sessions. We evaluate 12 recent LLMs under no-history and same-user-history conditions using executable success, first-turn success, and turns-to-completion. Our analyses examine task difficulty, user identity, and memory-based history use, and we further propose same-user history gating as a lightweight inference-time method. CAPA provides a foundation for developing long-term coding assistants that better align generated code with user intent while reducing repeated clarification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CAPA, a benchmark for personalized ambiguity adaptation in AI-assisted coding, where recurring user-specific ambiguities across sessions should be resolved using previously resolved session history. It formulates the task, proposes a six-mechanism ambiguity framework with a controlled generation pipeline (600 sessions, 60 user-ambiguity cells), evaluates 12 LLMs, and introduces same-user history gating.
AI.motivation: Coding requests often contain ambiguities that recur in user-specific ways across tasks and sessions. Existing methods address ambiguities in isolation within a single session, ignoring the potential of leveraging a user's resolved session history as memory to reduce repeated clarification.
AI.method: (1) Formulate personalized ambiguity adaptation as a new task; (2) Introduce CAPA benchmark with six ambiguity mechanisms injected via a controlled three-stage generation pipeline; (3) Evaluate 12 LLMs under no-history and same-user-history conditions using executable success, first-turn success, and turns-to-completion; (4) Propose same-user history gating as a lightweight inference-time method.
AI.result: CAPA contains 600 coding sessions across 60 balanced user-ambiguity cells with 300 held-out evaluation sessions. Evaluations cover 12 recent LLMs, comparing performance with and without same-user session history.
AI.conclusion: CAPA provides a foundation for developing long-term coding assistants that better align generated code with user intent while reducing repeated clarification, demonstrating that same-user session history can serve as effective memory for resolving recurring personalized ambiguity.

title: Eddeep: a deep-learning framework for fast eddy-current distortion correction in diffusion MRI
summary: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) relies on diffusion-weighted echo-planar imaging, which is highly susceptible to eddy-current-induced geometric distortions. These distortions vary across diffusion volumes according to gradient strength and direction, causing between-volume misalignment that can bias downstream microstructural analyses. Current state-of-the-art correction methods, such as FSL Eddy, achieve high-quality correction through iterative prediction-correction schemes but are computationally expensive. We propose Eddeep, a deep-learning framework for fast eddy-current distortion correction in dMRI. Eddeep decomposes the problem into two stages. First, a supervised image translation network standardises the appearance of diffusion-weighted and b=0 images, removing contrast differences that hinder reliable registration. Second, an unsupervised registration network estimates both eddy-current distortion and between-volume head motion parameters under a physics-constrained quadratic distortion model, enabling correction in a single forward pass. The method was trained on UK Biobank data and evaluated on both in-domain (UK Biobank) and out-of-domain (Memodyn) datasets. Across a range of complementary metrics, including between-volume jitter, diffusion kurtosis imaging residuals, signal irregularity, and mutual information, Eddeep achieved correction quality comparable to that of FSL Eddy while substantially reducing inference time. These results demonstrate that deep learning can provide accurate and efficient eddy-current distortion correction without relying on iterative optimisation, supporting the development of faster diffusion MRI processing pipelines for large-scale studies and clinical deployment. The code is available at: https://github.com/CIG-UCL/eddeep.
