AI.tldr: Eddeep is a deep-learning framework for fast eddy-current distortion correction in diffusion MRI that decomposes the problem into supervised contrast normalization and unsupervised registration under a physics-constrained model, achieving correction quality comparable to FSL Eddy with substantially reduced inference time.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art eddy-current correction (FSL Eddy) uses iterative prediction-correction schemes that are computationally expensive, motivating the need for a faster deep-learning-based approach suitable for large-scale studies and clinical deployment.
AI.method: Eddeep uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) a supervised image translation network standardizes appearance between diffusion-weighted and b=0 images, and (2) an unsupervised registration network estimates eddy-current distortion and head motion parameters under a physics-constrained quadratic distortion model, performing correction in a single forward pass.
AI.result: Trained on UK Biobank and evaluated on both in-domain (UK Biobank) and out-of-domain (Memodyn) datasets. Across metrics such as between-volume jitter, DKI residuals, signal irregularity, and mutual information, Eddeep achieved correction quality comparable to FSL Eddy while substantially reducing inference time.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning can provide accurate and efficient eddy-current distortion correction without iterative optimization, supporting faster diffusion MRI processing pipelines for large-scale studies and clinical use.

title: A Scalable AI-Powered System for Explainable Machine Learning Pipelines in Brain Tumor
summary: Artificial intelligence and radiomics are increasingly used in brain tumor research, yet their translation into clinical practice remains limited by fragmented workflows, poor transparency, and weak integration with end users' needs. We present the first version of a scalable web-based visual analytics system designed to support radiomics-driven machine learning inference in neuro-oncology. The platform integrates three core functions within a single interface: cohort management from structured clinical tables, radiomic feature extraction from medical images and segmentation masks, and guarded inference with pre-trained machine learning models. The system was developed through an iterative user-centred design process and evaluated on both a public glioblastoma dataset and a proprietary clinical cohort. A key contribution is the explicit exposure of intermediate workflow artifacts, which improves traceability, interpretability, and responsible use of AI. By combining portability, inspectability, and deployment simplicity, the proposed framework offers a practical foundation for clinically oriented AI applications in brain tumor analysis.

AI.tldr: A scalable web-based visual analytics system integrating cohort management, radiomic feature extraction, and guarded ML inference for neuro-oncology, developed via user-centred design and evaluated on public and proprietary datasets, emphasizing traceability and interpretability for clinical AI translation.
AI.motivation: AI and radiomics in brain tumor research are limited in clinical translation due to fragmented workflows, poor transparency, and weak integration with end users' needs.
AI.method: Iterative user-centred design of a web-based visual analytics system with three core functions (cohort management, radiomic feature extraction, guarded ML inference), exposing intermediate workflow artifacts for traceability; evaluated on a public glioblastoma dataset and a proprietary clinical cohort.
AI.result: The system successfully integrates radiomics-driven ML inference in a portable, inspectable, and simple-to-deploy web interface, improving traceability, interpretability, and responsible AI use in brain tumor analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical foundation for clinically oriented AI applications in brain tumor analysis by combining portability, inspectability, and deployment simplicity.

title: High-Order Markov Blanket Discovery via a k-Order Relaxation of the Faithfulness Assumption
comment: 17 pages (9 pages main text + supplementary material), 4 figures, 8 tables, 3 algorithms. Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026). Code: https://github.com/lklee9/k-order-Markov-blanket
summary: The problem of learning the graphical Markov blanket (MB) of a variable from data has applications in many areas such as structure learning for Bayesian networks and Markov random fields, causal discovery, and feature selection. However, a common assumption most methods make is that the conditional independencies in the distribution imply the same separation in the graphical structure -- also known as the faithfulness assumption. Unfortunately, this assumption can be violated by higher-order dependencies such as XOR and parity-type relations, and -- on finite samples -- by empirical violations that, in extreme cases, even induce spurious dependencies absent from the true distribution. Therefore, in this paper we propose a "k-order" relaxation of the faithfulness assumption that captures parity type relationships between k+2 variables. We then propose a proof of concept algorithm called k-order Markov blanket (kOMB) that uses this relaxation for MB discovery. Finally, we empirically show how kOMB can recover the MB of a variable under both true and empirical violations of faithfulness. Code available at: https://github.com/lklee9/k-order-Markov-blanket

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a k-order relaxation of the faithfulness assumption to handle parity-type dependencies (like XOR) and empirical violations, and introduces the kOMB algorithm for Markov blanket discovery that works under such violations.
AI.motivation: Existing MB learning methods assume faithfulness, which is violated by higher-order dependencies (e.g., XOR, parity) and finite-sample empirical issues that can induce spurious dependencies, limiting their applicability.
AI.method: A k-order relaxation of the faithfulness assumption is introduced to capture parity-type relationships among k+2 variables. A proof-of-concept algorithm called k-order Markov blanket (kOMB) is proposed to leverage this relaxation for MB discovery.
AI.result: Empirical results demonstrate that kOMB can recover the Markov blanket under both true (structural) and empirical (finite-sample) violations of faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: The k-order relaxation and kOMB algorithm effectively extend MB discovery to settings where standard faithfulness fails, including parity-type dependencies and finite-sample violations.

title: AlphaSchema: Exploring the Space of Trading Semantics for LLM-Based Alpha Mining
summary: Automated alpha mining has increasingly adopted large language model (LLM) agents for factor generation and iterative discovery. However, existing LLM-based systems often delegate both factor construction and search decisions to the agent itself, without an explicit exploration space or a principled mechanism for navigating that space. As a result, exploration remains largely implicit and difficult to control or optimize systematically. We introduce AlphaSchema, which constructs and explores a structured space of trading semantics for alpha mining. Each point in this space is a schema plan composed of Event, Context, Qualities, Direction, and Output, specifying the semantics of a candidate factor before implementation. AlphaSchema decouples exploration from implementation: an LLM translates selected schema plans into executable factors, while evaluated rewards are accumulated to learn a surrogate model over the semantic space. An iterative selection mechanism uses this model to balance global exploration, surrogate-guided exploitation, and local mutation. Experiments on the Chinese stock market show that AlphaSchema discovers factor pools with strong predictive and portfolio performance. Further analyses show that the semantic search process navigates diverse regions while increasingly allocating evaluations toward high-reward regions, and that implementations of the same schema plans by different LLMs exhibit comparable predictive quality, suggesting that alpha mining quality is largely robust to the choice of LLM within our framework.

AI.tldr: AlphaSchema constructs a structured semantic space (Event, Context, Qualities, Direction, Output) for factor generation, decouples exploration from implementation, and uses a surrogate model with iterative selection to systematically navigate the space, demonstrating strong performance on Chinese stock markets.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based alpha mining systems lack explicit exploration spaces and principled mechanisms for navigating them, making exploration implicit and difficult to control or optimize systematically.
AI.method: AlphaSchema defines a structured semantic space where each point is a schema plan (Event, Context, Qualities, Direction, Output). It decouples exploration (surrogate model learning over semantics) from implementation (LLM translates plans to executable factors), using iterative selection that balances global exploration, surrogate-guided exploitation, and local mutation.
AI.result: AlphaSchema discovers factor pools with strong predictive and portfolio performance on the Chinese stock market. The semantic search navigates diverse regions while increasingly focusing on high-reward areas. Different LLMs implementing the same schema plans yield comparable predictive quality.
AI.conclusion: Alpha mining quality is largely robust to the choice of LLM within the proposed framework, and structured semantic exploration is effective for systematic factor discovery.

title: MoSAIC: Aligned Intervention Supervision for Part-Local Motion Style Transfer
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Project page: https://utsa-virlab.github.io/MoSAIC/
summary: Editing character motion often requires transferring a gesture or gait from one or more reference motions while preserving the source action, timing, root trajectory, and unselected body regions. Existing motion datasets, however, rarely provide paired targets for arbitrary part-local content--reference combinations, and self-reconstruction training may allow a diffusion model to reproduce the content motion while underusing the routed reference. We present MoSAIC, a latent diffusion framework for part-local reference-conditioned motion style transfer. MoSAIC factorizes content and reference features by anatomical region, preserves the root trajectory through a separate conditioning pathway, and routes user-selected references to individual body parts. Its central contribution is aligned intervention supervision, which constructs synchronized references and counterfactual targets through controlled local transformations, making both the requested regional response and the motion to be preserved directly observable during training. In a frozen evaluation comprising 128 motions and 896 routed conditions, part-masked routing reduces preserved-region error from 70.64 to 66.45~mm and matched-noise off-target leakage from 18.08 to 9.88~mm relative to whole-body routing, while retaining a positive selected-region response. A matched-budget continuation study further shows that retaining aligned intervention supervision produces an 8.8\% relative increase in selected-target response and a 2.0-percentage-point increase in requested-route influence concentration. These results demonstrate that MoSAIC improves the response--preservation trade-off required for selective and controllable part-local motion editing.

AI.tldr: MoSAIC is a latent diffusion framework for part-local motion style transfer that uses aligned intervention supervision to construct synchronized references and counterfactual targets, enabling selective body-part editing while preserving unselected regions. It reduces preserved-region error and off-target leakage compared to whole-body routing, and improves the response-preservation trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing motion datasets lack paired targets for arbitrary part-local content-reference combinations, and self-reconstruction training causes diffusion models to underuse routed references by reproducing content motion instead of applying the desired style transfer.
AI.method: MoSAIC uses a latent diffusion framework with anatomical region factorization of content and reference features, separate root trajectory conditioning, and user-selected reference routing to individual body parts. Its key technique is aligned intervention supervision, which creates synchronized references and counterfactual targets through controlled local transformations, making both the regional response and preserved motion directly observable during training.
AI.result: In frozen evaluation (128 motions, 896 conditions): part-masked routing reduced preserved-region error from 70.64 to 66.45 mm and matched-noise off-target leakage from 18.08 to 9.88 mm vs whole-body routing, while retaining positive selected-region response. Matched-budget continuation study showed 8.8% relative increase in selected-target response and 2.0-percentage-point increase in route influence concentration.
AI.conclusion: MoSAIC significantly improves the response-preservation trade-off for selective, controllable part-local motion editing, demonstrating effective part-local reference-conditioned motion style transfer.

title: When Knowledge Changes: Metamorphic Testing of RAG Systems with Mutations
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based LLM systems rely on external document corpora that can evolve and change over time. However, current evaluation methodologies (e.g., RAGAS) assess correctness against static snapshots, failing to detect faults when routine updates, factual changes, or noise alter the underlying data. We introduce a metamorphic testing framework that evaluates the consistency of RAG systems under corpus evolution. We formalise a fault taxonomy and 11 mutation operators that systematically perturb the system at both the pre-chunk (retrieval index) and post-chunk (retrieved context) levels. An empirical evaluation across five datasets and over 28k mutants reveals metamorphic violation rates of 4.9-10.2%. In a meta-evaluation against ground truth, our metamorphic oracle achieves F1 scores of 0.927-1.000, while the best RAGAS metric reaches only 0.570. Finally, we provide actionable insights into mitigating these faults through retrieval re-configuration, generator upgrades, and LLM-based reranking.

AI.tldr: A metamorphic testing framework for RAG-based LLM systems that detects faults caused by evolving document corpora, achieving high F1 scores (0.927-1.000) compared to existing metrics (max 0.570).
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methodologies (e.g., RAGAS) assess RAG systems against static snapshots, failing to detect faults when document corpora evolve through routine updates, factual changes, or noise introduction.
AI.method: Proposes a metamorphic testing framework with a formalized fault taxonomy and 11 mutation operators that perturb the RAG system at both pre-chunk (retrieval index) and post-chunk (retrieved context) levels. Evaluated across five datasets with over 28k mutants.
AI.result: Metamorphic violation rates of 4.9-10.2%. The metamorphic oracle achieves F1 scores of 0.927-1.000, while the best RAGAS metric reaches only 0.570.
AI.conclusion: Provides actionable insights for mitigating corpus-evolution faults through retrieval re-configuration, generator upgrades, and LLM-based reranking.

title: Post-Training at the Edge of Detectability: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Fine-Tuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning is widely used in language model training to improve model performance on a target task while limiting drift from a reference policy. A standard way to balance this trade-off is via a KL-regularized RL objective, although this formulation does not by itself provide a principled way to set the regularization coefficient. In practice, the coefficient is typically chosen heuristically or via hyperparameter search, which can lead to unnecessary overhead in training cost or undesirable reward-retention trade-offs. We instead propose a game-theoretic framework that gives this trade-off an explicit statistical interpretation. Specifically, we study a sequential game in which an agent chooses a policy to maximize cumulative reward while a monitor observes policy outputs over time and tests for deviations from the reference policy. Although not originating from the same perspective, we show that the resulting equilibrium policy can nonetheless be expressed as the solution to a KL-regularized RL problem for an optimal regularization parameter that can be viewed as maximizing reward per unit of statistical distinguishability. Drawing on classical results from concave-convex fractional programming, we provide a principled method for learning this equilibrium coefficient via reduction to the KL-regularized RL objective, thus allowing for flexible integration into standard fine-tuning pipelines. In experiments with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-1B, we demonstrate that our methods result in competitive reward-retention trade-offs in a continual learning setting, and illustrate how our framework may be used to audit API providers serving open-source models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a game-theoretic framework for KL-regularized RL fine-tuning that automatically determines the optimal regularization coefficient by interpreting it as maximizing reward per unit of statistical distinguishability, using concave-convex fractional programming to integrate into standard pipelines.
AI.motivation: The standard KL-regularized RL fine-tuning lacks a principled way to set the regularization coefficient, which is typically chosen heuristically or via costly hyperparameter search, leading to unnecessary training overhead or suboptimal reward-retention trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors formulate a sequential game between an agent (maximizing cumulative reward) and a monitor (testing for deviations from the reference policy). They show the equilibrium policy solves a KL-regularized RL problem with an optimal regularization parameter, and use concave-convex fractional programming to learn this coefficient via reduction to the standard KL-regularized RL objective.
AI.result: Experiments with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-1B demonstrate competitive reward-retention trade-offs in continual learning settings, and the framework can be used to audit API providers serving open-source models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed game-theoretic framework provides a principled, interpretable method for setting the KL regularization coefficient in RL fine-tuning, bridging statistical distinguishability and reward optimization while reducing heuristic hyperparameter tuning overhead.

title: Rethinking Self-Evolution: A Constrained Exploration-Exploitation Process for Mitigating Skill Overfitting
summary: Enabling large language model (LLM) agents to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions remains a central challenge in real-world applications. A promising solution is to treat skills as trainable states and optimize them in the same way as model parameters in neural network training. However, data-driven skill optimization is prone to overfitting to the limited trajectories collected from real environments. Overexploiting these trajectories overfits the current batch, while unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved cases. This tension motivates a constrained search view of skill self-evolution, governed by an exploration--exploitation trade-off. We propose SkillBoost, a three-stage framework that mitigates both risks: structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components, prior-guided exploration draws on prior knowledge in the LLM to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound. Experiments across 23 model--benchmark configurations show that SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills. Transfer experiments further show that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks.

AI.tldr: SkillBoost is a three-stage framework (structured exploitation, prior-guided exploration, verified acceptance) that enables LLM agents to optimize skills from past experiences while balancing exploration-exploitation to avoid overfitting, achieving SOTA across 23 model-benchmark configurations.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions; data-driven skill optimization suffers from overfitting to limited real-environment trajectories, and unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved tasks.
AI.method: SkillBoost is a three-stage framework: (1) structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components; (2) prior-guided exploration leverages prior knowledge in the LLM to generate diverse repair candidates; (3) verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance across 23 model-benchmark configurations while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills; optimized skills transfer to other agents on similar tasks.
AI.conclusion: Treating skills as trainable states with constrained search (exploration-exploitation trade-off) effectively enables skill self-evolution without overfitting; the framework produces reusable skills transferable across agents.

title: Seeing or Knowing? Visual Context Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance by integrating visual inputs with the rich priors of pretrained language models. However, they often fail on vision-centric tasks, especially when visual evidence conflicts with pretrained knowledge. We explore these failures separately using two diagnostic paradigms: (1) probing whether visual information is available, via image reconstruction, and (2) measuring multimodal context sensitivity, the extent to which the model follows visual context versus the language prior. To support the second, we introduce the WhatIfVis, a benchmark spanning five coarse-grained dimensions (spatial-temporal, color, count, size, and weight) whose questions admit answers from either the image or the prior. Our analysis yields three findings: (i) Coarse-grained visual evidence is preserved, as these attributes can be reconstructed from the final-layer image tokens of frozen MLLMs. Failures on questions about these attributes therefore point to post-perceptual utilization, rather than to degraded visual encoding during perception. (ii) Even when explicitly instructed to use or ignore visual evidence, vanilla models (without supervised fine-tuning on the WhatIfVis) show unstable visual context sensitivity. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) improves this controllability and generalizes across domains, and activation patching further localizes the vision-versus-prior trade-off at architecture-specific depths across all six models. (iii) The vision-versus-prior trade-off is controllable along a learned vector. Applying this steering vector, even without any intent instruction, improves controllability over the vanilla model. Together, these results relocate the bottleneck, indicating that for the coarse attributes we study, MLLMs encode the visual evidence but cannot reliably control their reliance on it.

AI.tldr: MLLMs encode coarse visual attributes (color, size, etc.) in their representations but fail to reliably control reliance on visual evidence vs. language priors; this bottleneck is addressable via SFT and activation steering.
AI.motivation: To understand why MLLMs fail on vision-centric tasks when visual evidence conflicts with pretrained language priors, and to localize whether the bottleneck lies in visual perception or post-perceptual utilization of that information.
AI.method: Two diagnostic paradigms: (1) image reconstruction from final-layer image tokens to probe visual information availability; (2) WhatIfVis benchmark spanning five coarse-grained dimensions (spatial-temporal, color, count, size, weight) to measure multimodal context sensitivity. Analysis uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT), activation patching, and learned steering vectors.
AI.result: (i) Coarse visual attributes are preserved in frozen MLLM representations (reconstructable from final-layer tokens). (ii) Vanilla models show unstable visual context sensitivity; SFT improves controllability and generalizes across domains; activation patching localizes the vision-prior trade-off at architecture-specific depths. (iii) The trade-off is controllable along a learned steering vector, improving controllability without explicit instructions.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck for coarse visual attributes is not visual encoding but unreliable control over reliance on visual evidence vs. language priors; this can be mitigated through SFT and activation steering.

title: VITAL-RAG: Invariance Race for Context Allocation in Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents often retrieve code from an entire repository, but only limited evidence can fit into the final model input. Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for coding agents treats fragments from the same code object as separate results, so redundant views can occupy multiple context positions and crowd out useful code. Grouping fragments by code object reduces this redundancy, but can discard local information needed for the task. We describe this tension as an invariance race: allocation should stay stable under redundant renderings but change when a fragment adds task-relevant semantics. To address this race, we introduce VITAL-RAG, which organizes evidence by canonical code object, keeps one query-relevant companion only when it adds semantics not already represented, and renders selected evidence under per-object and global token budgets. On RepoBench, VITALRAG improves Recall@4K from 39.59% to 63.67% while reducing evidence tokens by 35.63%. Across three model backends, it matches or outperforms recent baselines on RepoClassBench and achieves the highest raw Pass@1 on RepoExec.

AI.tldr: VITAL-RAG improves code retrieval for coding agents by organizing evidence by canonical code objects, reducing redundancy while preserving task-relevant semantics, achieving significant gains in Recall@4K (39.59% → 63.67%) with 35.63% fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Conventional RAG for coding agents treats fragments from the same code object as separate results, causing redundant views to occupy multiple context positions and crowd out useful code. Grouping by code object reduces redundancy but can discard local information. This tension is described as an "invariance race" between stable allocation under redundant renderings and sensitivity to task-relevant semantics.
AI.method: VITAL-RAG organizes evidence by canonical code object, keeps one query-relevant companion only when it adds novel semantics, and renders selected evidence under per-object and global token budgets.
AI.result: On RepoBench, Recall@4K improved from 39.59% to 63.67% with 35.63% fewer tokens. Across three model backends, VITAL-RAG matches or outperforms baselines on RepoClassBench and achieves highest raw Pass@1 on RepoExec.
AI.conclusion: VITAL-RAG effectively resolves the invariance race in code retrieval for coding agents by balancing redundancy reduction and semantic preservation, leading to more efficient and effective evidence selection.

title: ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) has been widely adopted in transformer-based large language models. However, its log-linear frequency schedule, originally designed to produce long-term attention decay, limits its adoption in domains with more complex distance-correlation patterns, such as temporal periodicity in sequential recommendation. We investigate the expressiveness of general query/key rotations and find that any normalized continuous positive-definite attention modulation function can be approximated by random rotations induced by its own Fourier transform, which we term Random Fourier Rotations. Building on this theory, we propose ClockRoPE for routine modeling in sequential recommendation, where rotation frequencies are derived from periodic attention modulation functions. In online A/B tests, ClockRoPE demonstrates consistent improvements in valued engagement metrics, and has been successfully deployed in production-scale generative retrieval system at a major video-sharing platform.

AI.tldr: ClockRoPE extends Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) by deriving rotation frequencies from periodic attention modulation functions, enabling effective routine modeling in sequential recommendation, with proven success in production A/B tests at a major video-sharing platform.
AI.motivation: RoPE's log-linear frequency schedule limits its applicability in domains requiring complex distance-correlation patterns (e.g., temporal periodicity in sequential recommendation).
AI.method: The authors theoretically show that any normalized continuous positive-definite attention modulation function can be approximated by random rotations induced by its own Fourier transform (Random Fourier Rotations). They propose ClockRoPE, which derives rotation frequencies from periodic attention modulation functions for routine modeling.
AI.result: ClockRoPE shows consistent improvements in valued engagement metrics in online A/B tests and has been successfully deployed in a production-scale generative retrieval system.
AI.conclusion: ClockRoPE effectively addresses RoPE's limitation in handling periodicity, proving its practical value in large-scale recommender systems.

title: AgenticCANN: Automated Ascend C Operator Generation via Knowledge-Augmented Agentic Evolution
summary: Ascend C operator optimization is critical for NPU (Neural Processing Unit) inference performance but requires deep hardware expertise.While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automated CUDA kernel generation, the fundamentally different programming model of Ascend C introduces unique challenges that remain unexplored. In this paper, we propose AgenticCANN, a knowledge-augmented agentic evolution framework specifically tailored for automated Ascend C operator synthesis in low-corpus NPU environments.To overcome the severe platform knowledge deficit on unfamiliar hardware, AgenticCANN incorporates a knowledge-orchestrated generation system that delivers structured, multi-level domain insights across the development lifecycle to resolve the upstream feasibility bottleneck.Building on this foundation, it features a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy that dynamically aligns LLM interaction modes with specific generation and evolution phases, balancing high-exploration candidate discovery with high-convergence performance tuning.Extensive experiments on Huawei Ascend 910B across six operators spanning five pattern categories demonstrate that our method achieves 90 to 100 percent feasibility on elementwise and normalization operators, 56% on fusion operators, and up to 6.65$\times$ speedup on 1B Pangu model inference kernels. Further analysis reveals that knowledge injection monotonically improves feasibility from 57% to 86% on elementwise operators, demonstrating its general rather than operator-specific benefit.

AI.tldr: AgenticCANN is a knowledge-augmented agentic evolution framework for automated Ascend C operator synthesis on NPU environments with limited corpus, achieving 90-100% feasibility on elementwise/normalization operators and up to 6.65× speedup on Huawei Ascend 910B.
AI.motivation: Ascend C operator optimization is critical for NPU inference but requires deep hardware expertise. While LLMs have succeeded in CUDA kernel generation, the fundamentally different programming model of Ascend C introduces unique challenges that remain unexplored due to a severe platform knowledge deficit on unfamiliar hardware.
AI.method: The framework includes: (1) a knowledge-orchestrated generation system delivering structured, multi-level domain insights across the development lifecycle to resolve upstream feasibility bottlenecks; and (2) a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy that dynamically aligns LLM interaction modes with specific generation and evolution phases, balancing high-exploration candidate discovery with high-convergence performance tuning.
AI.result: On Huawei Ascend 910B across six operators spanning five pattern categories, the method achieves 90-100% feasibility on elementwise and normalization operators, 56% on fusion operators, and up to 6.65× speedup on 1B Pangu model inference kernels. Knowledge injection monotonically improves feasibility from 57% to 86% on elementwise operators.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates that structured knowledge injection and stage-adaptive agentic evolution can effectively overcome the platform knowledge deficit in low-corpus NPU environments, with knowledge benefits being general rather than operator-specific.

title: Zero-Fi: Zero-Shot Wi-Fi-Based Human Activity Recognition via Contrastive Signal-Language Alignment
summary: Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition has advanced substantially, but most existing methods assume a closed set of activities and require labeled Wi-Fi samples for every target class, limiting their ability to recognize unseen activities. We present Zero-Fi, a contrastive signal-language alignment framework for zero-shot Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition. Zero-Fi learns unified representations from complementary Wi-Fi signal features and aligns them with the semantic representations of natural-language activity descriptions in a shared embedding space. This cross-modal alignment enables Zero-Fi to recognize new activity classes without requiring labeled Wi-Fi samples or model adaptation for those classes. Experiments on large-scale public benchmark datasets demonstrate effective zero-shot recognition of held-out activity classes, highlighting the potential of signal-language alignment to extend Wi-Fi sensing beyond predefined activity classes.

AI.tldr: Zero-Fi is a contrastive signal-language alignment framework that enables zero-shot Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition by learning unified representations from Wi-Fi signals and aligning them with natural-language activity descriptions, allowing recognition of unseen activities without labeled samples or model retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing Wi-Fi-based activity recognition methods assume a closed set of activities and require labeled Wi-Fi samples for every target class, which limits their ability to recognize unseen or novel activities.
AI.method: Zero-Fi uses a contrastive signal-language alignment framework that learns unified representations from complementary Wi-Fi signal features and aligns them with semantic representations of natural-language activity descriptions in a shared embedding space via cross-modal learning.
AI.result: Experiments on large-scale public benchmark datasets demonstrate effective zero-shot recognition of held-out activity classes.
AI.conclusion: Signal-language alignment can extend Wi-Fi sensing beyond predefined activity classes, enabling recognition of unseen activities without requiring labeled Wi-Fi samples or model adaptation.

title: How Developers Experience Debugging Unfamiliar Codebases with Code Tours Generated and Evaluated by Local LLMs
summary: Code tours are interactive, onboarding documentation to guide developers through a codebase. Large Language Models (LLMs) can automatically synthesize code tours. Prior work on code tour generation has not studied developer experience or trust calibration when debugging unfamiliar codebases with code tours generated and evaluated by open-weight LLMs. This study surveys how the properties of components in open-weight LLM-authored code tours influence developers' experiences when debugging unfamiliar codebases. We built a pipeline that generated and evaluated code tours from real reproducible bugs. 26 developers with varying backgrounds participated in a user study. In total, 26 code tours were authored from real Java bugs mined from 2025 GitHub commits, with each tour independently judged by two different LLMs, resulting in 52 evaluated configurations. Participants thought aloud as they explored each tour. Three authors qualitatively coded the interviews to identify recurring themes. Developers generally preferred tours that scaled detail with the code length, avoided merely restating code, were easily scannable, and adopted a guiding tone. However, some preferences were mutually exclusive, such as the use of imperative mood. Stack traces were often insufficient to identify all steps developers found relevant. Developers also trusted descriptions they perceived as human-written more than those they believed were AI-generated. Finally, LLM-generated annotations of tour quality were unreliable: sycophancy, confabulation, and incoherence were pervasive. This work lays a basis for future research on fine-tuning open-weight models for code tour generation, personalizing generation to accommodate diverging preferences, selecting relevant steps beyond stack traces, calibrating users' trust to avoid both disuse and misuse, and improving open-weight LLMs' ability to be more trustworthy evaluators

AI.tldr: This study investigates how properties of open-weight LLM-authored code tours influence developers' debugging experiences through a user study with 26 developers, finding preferences for context-appropriate detail, scannability, and guiding tone, while revealing issues with trust calibration, LLM self-evaluation unreliability (sycophancy, confabulation, incoherence), and mutually exclusive preferences.
AI.motivation: Prior work on code tour generation has not studied developer experience or trust calibration when debugging unfamiliar codebases with code tours generated and evaluated by open-weight LLMs, leaving a gap in understanding how properties of LLM-authored tours affect real developer workflows.
AI.method: Built a pipeline to generate and evaluate code tours from real reproducible bugs mined from 2025 GitHub commits (Java); conducted a user study with 26 developers (52 evaluated configurations via two LLM judges); used think-aloud protocol and qualitative coding by three authors to identify recurring themes.
AI.result: Developers preferred tours that scale detail with code length, avoid restating code, are scannable, and use a guiding tone. Mutually exclusive preferences (e.g., imperative mood) existed. Stack traces insufficient for identifying all relevant steps. Developers trusted human-written descriptions over AI-generated ones. LLM-generated quality annotations were unreliable due to sycophancy, confabulation, and incoherence.
AI.conclusion: Lays basis for future research on fine-tuning open-weight models for code tour generation, personalization to accommodate diverging preferences, selecting relevant steps beyond stack traces, calibrating user trust, and improving open-weight LLMs as trustworthy evaluators.

title: Q-Steer: Action-Value Guidance for Molecular Policy Optimization
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, and 25 tables. Includes supplementary experimental results
summary: Oracle-limited molecular optimization gives reward only after a complete molecule is generated, while each rollout requires many local next-token decisions. This delayed-feedback interface makes molecular policy optimization myopic: an optimizer can learn that a molecule was good without knowing which intermediate actions made it good. We introduce Q-Steer, a rollout-time action-value steering primitive for molecular language models. Q-Steer uses an offline-trained and frozen prefix-action value scorer, PAVS-Q, that estimates the downstream reward of taking a candidate next token under a partial SMILES prefix, then adds a normalized value bonus to sampling logits. The optimizer update rule and online oracle budget are unchanged; the claim is fixed-online-oracle performance, not equal total compute. On PMO23 with a fixed 10,000-call online budget, complete factorial studies across two molecular language-model backbones and four optimizers show that Q-Steer improves mean valid-unique score in all eight backbone-optimizer cells, with positive macro mean-score gains between +0.033 and +0.049 and 18-20 task wins per cell. Mechanism controls show that action identity matters: prefix-broadcast values are nearly neutral, while shuffled action values harm performance. These results support Q-Steer as a reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that improves average molecular optimization reward across optimizer families and policy backbones without changing the online oracle budget.

AI.tldr: Q-Steer is a rollout-time action-value steering primitive for molecular language models that improves molecular optimization by adding value bonuses to sampling logits using an offline-trained prefix-action value scorer, without changing the online oracle budget.
AI.motivation: Molecular policy optimization suffers from delayed feedback: reward is only given after a complete molecule is generated, making it myopic since the optimizer cannot discern which intermediate actions contributed to the final good molecule.
AI.method: Q-Steer uses an offline-trained and frozen prefix-action value scorer (PAVS-Q) to estimate the downstream reward of a candidate next token under a partial SMILES prefix, then adds a normalized value bonus to the sampling logits during rollout time. The optimizer update rule and online oracle budget remain unchanged.
AI.result: On PMO23 with a fixed 10,000-call online budget, Q-Steer improves mean valid-unique score in all 8 backbone-optimizer combinations, with positive macro mean-score gains between +0.033 and +0.049 and 18-20 task wins per cell. Mechanism controls show prefix-broadcast values are nearly neutral while shuffled action values harm performance.
AI.conclusion: Q-Steer serves as a reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that improves average molecular optimization reward across different optimizer families and policy backbones without altering the online oracle budget.

title: UrbanDS: A Graph-Guided LLM Multi-Agent System for Data-Intensive Urban Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have been widely applied in automating data science tasks. However, existing methods typically rely on a limited set of provided datasets, and they face challenges in data-intensive scenarios that require discovering and leveraging relevant information from large-scale and heterogeneous data repositories. Urban tasks are representative examples of such scenarios, as urban data are not only large-scale and multi-sourced, but also exhibit complex spatial, temporal, and semantic relationships. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanDS, a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system for data-intensive urban tasks. We first construct a unified dataset graph to organize reusable dataset skills and the relationships among datasets. Specifically, we develop a Data Profiling Agent that constructs a skill for each dataset. Moreover, a Relation Agent identifies relationships among datasets and integrates these relationships into the dataset graph. At runtime, a Planner Agent retrieves task-relevant datasets from the graph and generates execution plans. Multiple Execution Agents then perform data processing and analysis, while their execution progress and intermediate results are shared through a common memory. Finally, a Report Agent synthesizes the experimental logs into a report, which can be further refined based on user feedback. To systematically evaluate the capability of agents in handling data-intensive urban scenarios, we further construct UrbanDS-Bench, an urban data science benchmark covering representative data analysis and modeling tasks. Experiments on both general and urban benchmarks demonstrate that UrbanDS consistently outperforms existing data science agents on data-intensive tasks. Furthermore, UrbanDS has been deployed on the urban operations platform of Dongxihu District, Wuhan, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world urban applications.

AI.tldr: UrbanDS is a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system for data-intensive urban tasks that organizes datasets via a unified graph with profiling and relation agents, plans and executes tasks through specialized agents, and outperforms existing agents on benchmarks, with real-world deployment in Wuhan.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for data science rely on limited provided datasets and struggle with large-scale, heterogeneous, multi-sourced urban data that has complex spatial, temporal, and semantic relationships.
AI.method: UrbanDS constructs a unified dataset graph via a Data Profiling Agent (skill extraction) and a Relation Agent (relationship identification). At runtime, a Planner Agent retrieves relevant datasets and generates plans, multiple Execution Agents process data with shared memory via a common memory, and a Report Agent synthesizes results into a report with user feedback refinement.
AI.result: UrbanDS consistently outperforms existing data science agents on both general and urban benchmarks (UrbanDS-Bench), and has been successfully deployed on the urban operations platform of Dongxihu District, Wuhan showing real-world effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The graph-guided multi-agent approach effectively addresses data-intensive urban scenarios by organizing heterogeneous datasets and their relationships, enabling scalable and reusable data science automation.

title: Registration-Grounded Spectral Fusion for Unregistered WLI/NBI Endoscopic Lesion Segmentation
summary: White-light imaging (WLI) and narrow-band imaging (NBI) provide complementary views of endoscopic lesions, but their paired observations are often spatially misaligned due to viewpoint changes, tissue deformation, and sequential handheld acquisition. This makes direct WLI/NBI fusion prone to mixing non-corresponding regions and may even degrade segmentation around lesion boundaries. To address this problem, we propose a reliability-aware complex-domain fusion framework for paired-but-unregistered WLI/NBI lesion segmentation. The framework first establishes topology-regularized feature correspondence and further estimates where the cross-modal correspondence is reliable. Guided by this reliability, the model selectively fuses WLI and NBI features in a learnable complex representation. In this representation, WLI-derived cues mainly provide appearance-related magnitude responses, while NBI-derived cues provide structure-sensitive phase responses. Unlike conventional real-valued or symmetric multimodal fusion, the proposed method explicitly models the different roles of WLI and NBI and suppresses unreliable cross-modal interaction in locally mismatched regions. Experiments on paired WLI/NBI endoscopic datasets show that the proposed reliability-aware registration grounding and complex-domain fusion consistently improve lesion segmentation performance. Role-reversal and module ablation studies further validate the necessity of both the modality-role design and reliability-guided cross-modal interaction.

AI.tldr: A reliability-aware complex-domain fusion framework for segmenting lesions from unregistered WLI and NBI endoscopic images, using topology-regularized correspondence and complex-valued features where WLI contributes magnitude responses and NBI contributes phase responses.
AI.motivation: WLI and NBI provide complementary views but are spatially misaligned due to viewpoint changes, tissue deformation, and handheld acquisition, causing direct fusion to mix non-corresponding regions and degrade segmentation around lesion boundaries.
AI.method: The framework has two main components: (1) topology-regularized feature correspondence to establish cross-modal alignment and estimate reliability of correspondence; (2) complex-domain fusion where WLI provides appearance-related magnitude responses and NBI provides structure-sensitive phase responses, with reliability-guided selective fusion suppressing interaction in mismatched regions.
AI.result: Experiments on paired WLI/NBI endoscopic datasets show consistent improvement in lesion segmentation performance. Role-reversal and ablation studies validate the necessity of the modality-role design and reliability-guided cross-modal interaction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively handles the spatial misalignment between WLI and NBI by explicitly modeling their complementary roles (appearance vs. structure) in complex domain and suppressing unreliable cross-modal interactions, outperforming conventional real-valued or symmetric fusion approaches.

title: MindForge: Teaching Small Language Models Whole-Life-Cycle Software Engineering via Source-Free Program Synthesis
summary: Coding agents have made substantial progress on software engineering tasks that modify existing codebases, including bug fixing and feature implementation. However, constructing a complete program from scratch remains a major challenge: even the frontier models evaluated on ProgramBench fully resolve fewer than 1% of tasks. One obstacle is the lack of scalable training environments for this from-scratch setting, spanning the whole software engineering life cycle, as existing environment-construction frameworks focus only on a single phase in software development. To address this gap, we introduce MindForge, an automated pipeline that converts open-source command-line programs into source-free environments that expose only a compiled reference executable and its documentation. Using MindForge, we construct training environments from repositories disjoint from those in ProgramBench, and curate a high-quality data recipe consisting of program synthesis trajectories using GLM-5.2 as the teacher agent. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B on these trajectories increases its ProgramBench average test pass rate from 37.98% to 49.51%, achieving performance comparable to substantially larger frontier models. Moreover, the fine-tuned model consistently improves over the base model across all seven unseen software engineering benchmarks, spanning long-horizon repository generation and translation, bug fixing, feature implementation, and cross-language issue resolution, with absolute gains of 31.00 points on RepoZero-C2Rust, 14.16 on DeepSWE, 10.70/4.56 on NL2Repo-Bench (with/without tests), 5.04 on SWE-bench Verified, 5.93 on SWE-bench Pro, 5.22 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 4.94 on FeatBench.

AI.tldr: MindForge is an automated pipeline converting open-source command-line programs into source-free training environments for from-scratch coding agents. Using it, they train Qwen3.6-27B with GLM-5.2-generated trajectories, boosting ProgramBench pass rate from 37.98% to 49.51%, and achieving consistent gains across 7 software engineering benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Coding agents struggle with constructing complete programs from scratch (less than 1% resolution on ProgramBench). The lack of scalable training environments covering the full software engineering lifecycle is a key obstacle, as existing frameworks focus only on single development phases.
AI.method: MindForge: an automated pipeline converting open-source CLI programs into source-free environments (compiled reference executable + documentation only). Training environments built from repos disjoint from ProgramBench. Data recipe: program synthesis trajectories generated by GLM-5.2 teacher agent. Fine-tuned Qwen3.6-27B on these trajectories.
AI.result: ProgramBench average test pass rate improved from 37.98% to 49.51%. Consistent gains across 7 unseen benchmarks: RepoZero-C2Rust (+31.00), DeepSWE (+14.16), NL2Repo-Bench (+10.70/+4.56), SWE-bench Verified (+5.04), SWE-bench Pro (+5.93), SWE-bench Multilingual (+5.22), FeatBench (+4.94).
AI.conclusion: MindForge enables scalable training for from-scratch programming tasks. Fine-tuning with its generated data yields performance comparable to substantially larger frontier models and generalizes across diverse software engineering benchmarks.

title: Flow Map Learning via Nongradient Vector Flow
summary: Diffusion and flow-based models benefit from simple regression losses, but inference incurs significant overhead because sampling requires integration. Consistency models address this by directly learning the flow maps along the ODE trajectory, opening a design space between one-step and many-step approaches. However, existing methods face computational challenges such as requiring model inverses or backpropagation through iterated model calls, and do not always prove that the desired ODE flow map is a solution to the loss. We introduce SGFlow, an approach for learning flow maps that bypasses explicit invertibility constraints and expensive differentiation through model iteration. SGFlow trains a model to compute both the ODE solutions and the implied velocity from scratch by following non-conservative dynamics with a stationary point at the desired flow map. On the CIFAR image benchmark, no single method attains the best FID at every step count: SGFlow attains the best FID at 10 sampling steps and remains competitive with flow matching, Meanflow, and Lagrangian map matching at other step counts, while being the only one with a proven stationary-point guarantee for its stopgrad-based dynamics.

AI.tldr: SGFlow is a new method for learning flow maps in generative modeling that avoids invertibility constraints and expensive backpropagation, achieving competitive FID scores on CIFAR with theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing consistency models and flow-based methods suffer from computational overhead due to requiring model inverses or backpropagation through iterated model calls, and lack theoretical proof that the desired ODE flow map is a solution to the loss function.
AI.method: SGFlow trains a model to compute both ODE solutions and implied velocity from scratch by following non-conservative dynamics with a stationary point at the desired flow map, using stopgrad-based dynamics.
AI.result: On CIFAR, SGFlow achieves the best FID at 10 sampling steps, and remains competitive with flow matching, Meanflow, and Lagrangian map matching at other step counts. It is the only method with a proven stationary-point guarantee.
AI.conclusion: SGFlow provides a principled and efficient approach for learning flow maps without explicit invertibility or expensive differentiation, with theoretical guarantees and competitive empirical performance.

title: Do Latent Channels Actually Communicate? A Causal Audit of Latent Multi-Agent LLM
summary: Latent communication in large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) transmits continuous internal representations instead of text, but greater representational capacity does not establish that the receiver uses task-relevant information. End-task performance alone also cannot reveal whether an observed effect depends on message presence, content generated for the evaluated example, or information supplied by a separate agent. We introduce a causal audit that applies controlled message replacements at the boundary where the sender-produced representation enters the receiver. Four message settings support five measurements of encoded sender information, receiver sensitivity to message presence and identity, the task value of example-specific content, and the additional value supplied by a separate agent. We apply the audit to latent relay with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500. On GSM8K, the Qwen3-4B overall performance effect of -1.00 percentage point decomposes into a -6.17-point effect retained by an other-example message and a +5.17-point effect attributable to example-specific content; both component directions reverse at 8B. On MATH-500, the Qwen3-4B gain of 15.00 points comprises 8.33 points retained by an other-example message and 6.67 points attributable to example-specific content, while the 8B gain is dominated by the former component. Self-substitution comparisons further show that example-specific content and other-agent value are distinct. These results show that aggregate accuracy does not identify how a latent message affects the receiver and motivate controlled message comparisons as a standard evaluation for latent communication.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a causal audit to decompose how latent (continuous) communication affects receiver performance in LLM-based multi-agent systems. Applying it to Qwen3 models on three reasoning benchmarks, they find that aggregate accuracy masks opposing contributions from example-specific content vs. generic message presence, and that these effects differ by model size and dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of latent communication in LLM-based MAS cannot distinguish whether performance effects stem from message presence, example-specific content, or information from a separate agent; aggregate accuracy alone is insufficient to understand causal mechanisms.
AI.method: A causal audit with four message settings (sender-produced, other-example, self-substitution, fixed-baseline) and five measurements, applied at the sender-receiver boundary with controlled message replacements. Tested on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500.
AI.result: On GSM8K, Qwen3-4B's -1.00pp overall effect decomposes into -6.17pp from message presence and +5.17pp from example-specific content (reversed at 8B). On MATH-500, Qwen3-4B's +15.00pp gain splits into +8.33pp message-presence and +6.67pp example-specific content; 8B gain dominated by message-presence. Self-substitution confirms example-specific content and other-agent value are distinct.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate accuracy hides how latent messages causally affect receiver performance; controlled message comparisons should become a standard evaluation practice for latent communication.

title: Do Unified Multimodal Models Think in One Space? A Lens Through Cross-Branch Steering
summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) aim to integrate understanding and generation within a single architecture, yet it remains unclear whether these capabilities share a unified and transferable semantic space. This question is fundamentally challenging, as the two branches operate over heterogeneous representations (text tokens vs.\ visual latents) and distinct training objectives, making direct comparison difficult. To address this, we introduce \emph{cross-branch semantic steering}, an intervention-based framework that extracts semantic directions from one branch and applies them to the other. We show that steering vectors learned from the understanding branch can transfer to generation, enabling controllable image synthesis and improved semantic faithfulness. In contrast, the reverse direction consistently shows limited effectiveness. Our analysis suggests that this asymmetry may be related to a practical representational mismatch: understanding-derived vectors capture transferable, object-centric semantics, while generation-derived vectors primarily encode low-level appearance features. Our results reveal that architectural unification does not guarantee semantic alignment, and establish cross-branch steering as a practical tool for probing multimodal representations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether understanding and generation capabilities in unified multimodal models share a transferable semantic space, finding that steering vectors from understanding to generation enable controllable synthesis and improved faithfulness, but the reverse direction fails due to a representational mismatch (object-centric semantics vs. low-level appearance).
AI.motivation: To determine whether understanding and generation in UMMs share a unified and transferable semantic space, a fundamentally challenging question due to heterogeneous representations and distinct training objectives.
AI.method: Proposes cross-branch semantic steering, an intervention-based framework that extracts semantic directions from one branch and applies them to the other, probing transferability between understanding and generation.
AI.result: Understanding-to-generation steering enables controllable image synthesis and improved semantic faithfulness; generation-to-understanding steering shows limited effectiveness. This asymmetry stems from understanding vectors encoding transferable, object-centric semantics while generation vectors encode low-level appearance features.
AI.conclusion: Architectural unification does not guarantee semantic alignment; cross-branch steering is a practical tool for probing multimodal representations.

title: SpecFirst: Behavioral Specification Elicitation as a First-Class Step in Agent-Based Program Synthesis from Scratch
summary: LLM-based agents excel at software engineering tasks where an existing codebase provides context, but constructing a program from scratch remains fundamentally harder. Recent benchmarks such as ProgramBench quantify this gap: given only natural-language documentation and an execute-only binary as a behavioral oracle, even frontier models solve fewer than 1% of instances. Existing frameworks conflate documentation reading, behavioral exploration, and code synthesis into a single pass, causing agents to probe insufficiently, lose behavioral intent as context drifts, and propagate early misinterpretations into the final implementation. Inspired by classical requirements engineering, we argue that behavioral specification elicitation should be a first-class phase that precedes implementation. We present SpecFirst, a two-stage framework that forces the specification elicitation before code synthesis. A dedicated spec agent first probes the binary and combines observations with documentation into a structured specification. Next, a code synthesis agent then uses this specification to drive implementation. This decomposition resolves documentation ambiguities before coding begins and provides a stable behavioral reference throughout synthesis. We evaluate SpecFirst on all 200 ProgramBench instances across four models spanning two families and an order of magnitude of capability. SpecFirst consistently outperforms the single-loop baseline, improving test pass rates by 6.9%-21.3% and binary exploration coverage by 9.4%-18.5%, all statistically significant. Behavioral analysis on code synthesis further shows that a prior specification enables earlier and more sustained code construction. Our results demonstrate that an explicit requirements-engineering phase is an effective paradigm for from-scratch program construction.

AI.tldr: SpecFirst is a two-stage framework for LLM-based agents that separates behavioral specification elicitation from code synthesis, dramatically improving performance on from-scratch program construction tasks (6.9%-21.3% higher test pass rates) by resolving documentation ambiguities before coding begins.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle with constructing programs from scratch (vs. editing existing codebases), with frontier models solving <1% of ProgramBench instances. Existing single-loop frameworks conflate documentation reading, behavioral exploration, and code synthesis, causing insufficient probing, context drift, and propagation of early misinterpretations into final implementations.
AI.method: SpecFirst is a two-stage framework: (1) a dedicated spec agent probes the execute-only binary and combines observations with documentation into a structured specification; (2) a code synthesis agent uses this specification to drive implementation. This decomposition makes specification elicitation a first-class phase preceding implementation, inspired by classical requirements engineering.
AI.result: Evaluated on all 200 ProgramBench instances across 4 models (2 families, order-of-magnitude capability range). SpecFirst consistently outperforms single-loop baseline: test pass rates improve by 6.9%-21.3%, binary exploration coverage by 9.4%-18.5% (all statistically significant). Prior specification enables earlier and more sustained code construction.
AI.conclusion: An explicit requirements-engineering phase (specification elicitation before implementation) is an effective paradigm for from-scratch program construction with LLM-based agents.

title: Examining the Efficacy of Graph Neural Network Message-Passing in Regression Contexts
summary:
Graph Neural Networks (GNN) facilitate effective prediction on graph data such as molecules, media networks and neural network blueprints. GNNs facilitate prediction through message passing techniques which define how information flows from a node to its neighbors. Due to the ubiquity of the graph data type, the development of newer and better GNNs has garnered much interest in the machine learning community.
  However, GNN evaluation and benchmarking is primarily driven by classification tasks. Thus, prospective GNN message passing layers are evaluated on their ability to outperform prior work in classification contexts. In contrast, GNNs are equally capable of performing scalar regression prediction, yet this class of problem is often overlooked when proposing new GNNs while the best classification GNNs are utilized in an a priori or off-the-shelf manner for regression problems. In response, this paper studies the efficacy of GNN layers in a slew of regression contexts from rank ordering, error minimization and insight extraction. Results show that deep convolutional GNNs, particularly GEN, are more effective at these tasks than attention-based GNNs, while other classical, theoretically-inspired GNNs remain competitive and efficient.

AI.tldr: This paper studies GNN performance in regression tasks (rather than the typical classification focus) and finds that deep convolutional GNNs like GEN outperform attention-based GNNs, while classical theoretically-inspired GNNs remain competitive and efficient.
AI.motivation: GNN evaluation is dominated by classification benchmarks, yet GNNs are equally capable of regression tasks. New GNN layers are rarely validated on regression problems, leading to off-the-shelf use of classification-optimized GNNs for regression without proper justification.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate various GNN message passing layers across multiple regression contexts, including rank ordering, error minimization, and insight extraction, comparing deep convolutional GNNs, attention-based GNNs, and classical theoretically-inspired GNNs.
AI.result: Deep convolutional GNNs, particularly GEN (Graph Exchange Network), are more effective than attention-based GNNs for regression tasks. Classical theoretically-inspired GNNs remain competitive and computationally efficient.
AI.conclusion: GNN regression performance should be considered when proposing new message passing layers, as the best classification GNNs are not necessarily optimal for regression. Deep convolutional architectures like GEN are recommended for regression problems.

title: Property-driven Causal Abstractions for Markov Decision Processes
summary: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are widely used as decision-making models, commonly specified over factored state spaces through state variables and their valuations. The exponential blowup in the number of states renders many reasoning tasks in MDPs challenging. Abstractions are promising techniques to reduce MDPs and thus mitigate scalability issues. In this work, we introduce a notion of causality on factored MDPs and a novel property-driven causal abstraction technique that retains many characteristics of the original MDP model. For this, we rely on causal relations over state variable predicates and identify those states that share the same reasons for fulfilling or violating a given abstraction property. We theoretically and empirically compare various causal MDP abstractions using different model types such as MDPs, interval MDPs, or stochastic games. Our evaluation demonstrates the potential of our approach: For several standard benchmarks, we obtain small abstractions that allow us to compute near-optimal policies for the original MDP. Furthermore, our causal abstractions often generalize to related large-scale MDP models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a causality-based abstraction technique for factored MDPs that identifies states sharing the same reasons for satisfying or violating a property, enabling small abstractions that support near-optimal policy computation and generalization to larger models.
AI.motivation: Factored MDPs suffer from exponential state space blowup, making reasoning tasks challenging. Existing abstraction techniques help but often lose important model characteristics.
AI.method: The authors define causal relations over state variable predicates to identify states with shared reasons for property satisfaction/violation, and use these to construct property-driven causal abstractions. They compare different abstraction types (MDPs, interval MDPs, stochastic games).
AI.result: Small abstractions are obtained for standard benchmarks, enabling computation of near-optimal policies. The causal abstractions often generalize to related large-scale MDP models.
AI.conclusion: Causal abstraction is an effective technique for reducing factored MDPs while preserving key characteristics, with good generalization properties to larger models.

title: When Fish Look Alike: Tracking Identities with Dual-branch Elasticity
summary: Tracking dense, homogeneous targets like schooling fish remains a major challenge for multiple object tracking due to extreme inter-individual homogeneity, severe physical clustering, and rapid non-rigid deformations. While heavy-backbone separated detection and embedding trackers like SU-T push accuracy boundaries using complex Re-Identification networks, their computational overhead prohibits edge deployment. Furthermore, these modules often fail when appearance features degrade under severe occlusions. To overcome this, we propose Tracking Identities with Dual-branch Elasticity (TIDE). Bypassing expensive appearance cues, TIDE utilizes the Adaptive Geometric Correspondence IoU, an association mechanism leveraging spatial and structural consistency to robustly handle complex morphological variations. Crucially, TIDE introduces system-level deployment elasticity, decoupling the algorithmic pipeline from strict hardware constraints. Evaluations on the MFT-Edge benchmark demonstrate that our Lightweight L-branch achieves a competitive HOTA of 28.43 using merely 20.47G FLOPs. This represents a 38.7-fold computational reduction compared to upper bounds like SU-T, directly facilitating real-time edge deployment. Concurrently, our Scalable S-branch establishes a 29.98 HOTA, successfully bridging the gap between high-precision cloud analysis and efficient edge tracking. The dataset and codes are released at https://vranlee.github.io/TIDE/.

AI.tldr: TIDE introduces a dual-branch tracking framework (Lightweight L-branch for edge and Scalable S-branch for cloud) that uses Adaptive Geometric Correspondence IoU to track dense homogeneous targets like schooling fish without expensive appearance-based Re-Identification, achieving 38.7× FLOPs reduction vs. SU-T while maintaining competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing heavy-backbone detection+embedding trackers (e.g., SU-T) achieve high accuracy for dense homogeneous targets but their computational cost prohibits edge deployment, and appearance-based Re-Identification fails under severe occlusions.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive Geometric Correspondence IoU for spatial/structural association without appearance cues, along with a dual-branch architecture (L-branch for lightweight edge deployment, S-branch for scalable high-precision cloud analysis) with system-level deployment elasticity.
AI.result: L-branch achieves 28.43 HOTA with 20.47G FLOPs (38.7× reduction vs SU-T); S-branch achieves 29.98 HOTA, bridging cloud-edge performance gap.
AI.conclusion: TIDE demonstrates that bypassing expensive Re-ID features with geometric correspondence enables real-time edge tracking of dense homogeneous targets while a scalable branch can match high-precision cloud requirements, offering a practical elastic deployment solution.

title: SCOUT: Per-Context Reset Curricula for Sparse-Reward Reinforcement Learning
summary: Sparse-reward reinforcement learning often fails because rollouts from the unassisted evaluation start rarely reach later task stages. Reset curricula address this by starting some training rollouts from easier intermediate states, called scaffolds. Such a curriculum faces two decisions: scaffold access, obtaining informative starts, and scaffold allocation, deciding how quickly that assistance is removed. Most prior curricula pace removal on one shared schedule, which can fail when task instances, or contexts, learn at different rates. We introduce SCOUT, an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that gives every context its own curriculum. Using only binary rollout success, SCOUT removes assistance after sustained success, restores it after failure, and cautiously tests a harder start when progress stalls, without changing the reward, optimizer, or learner. A counting construction shows that synchronized global pacing can be insufficient when contexts need conflicting amounts of assisted practice. Across six navigation and manipulation settings, scaffold access improves learning and enables success in three where unassisted training fails within the reported budget. In a constructed pacing conflict, each tested global schedule leaves one group unsolved, while SCOUT solves both. Average success can conceal this failure, so we also report the least successful group. Group-level pacing works when learning differences follow known groups but can fail when they occur within one group. SCOUT needs no group labels and remains consistently strong in both cases. A reset curriculum should remove assistance at the scale where learning progress differs.

AI.tldr: SCOUT is an online reset controller that provides per-context curricula for sparse-reward RL, adapting scaffold removal to individual learning rates, outperforming global schedules especially when contexts learn at different paces.
AI.motivation: Sparse-reward RL often fails because unassisted rollouts rarely reach later task stages. Reset curricula can help via scaffolds, but prior work uses a single global schedule for removing assistance, which fails when different task instances (contexts) learn at different rates.
AI.method: SCOUT is an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that assigns each context its own curriculum. Using only binary rollout success, it removes assistance after sustained success, restores it after failure, and cautiously tests harder starts when progress stalls, without modifying the reward, optimizer, or learner.
AI.result: Across six navigation and manipulation tasks, SCOUT improves learning and succeeds in three where unassisted training fails. In a constructed pacing conflict, global schedules leave one group unsolved while SCOUT solves both. Group-level pacing fails when learning differences occur within a group; SCOUT requires no group labels and performs well in both cases.
AI.conclusion: A reset curriculum should remove assistance at the scale where learning progress differs. SCOUT's per-context pacing is crucial when contexts require conflicting amounts of assisted practice, and average success metrics can conceal group-level failures.

title: From Passive Video to Editable Experience: Physically Grounded Experience Synthesis for Embodied Intelligence
summary: The key bottleneck in embodied AI is not model architecture but data. Although billions of human manipulation videos exist online, robots cannot directly learn from them due to the embodiment gap between human morphology and robot hardware. We introduce Pegasus, a low-resource framework that bridges this gap by translating human demonstrations into robot-learnable data through structured knowledge transfer. Instead of relying on raw video prompts, Pegasus constructs a graph-based intermediate representation: a Task Graph extracted from human videos is transformed through Affordance and Constraint Graphs into a Robot Planning Graph for robot-conditioned video generation. A hierarchical affordance latent space models the relationship between object states, affordances, and tasks, enabling generalization beyond object identities. A closed-loop physics verifier further filters invalid generations using kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits. We evaluate Pegasus across a range of egocentric manipulation benchmarks, including GTEA Gaze+ and EPIC-KITCHENS-100, and diverse robot embodiments, assessing Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability. Results demonstrate reliable cross-embodiment translation and show that robot data generation can be reframed from a hardware collection problem into a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem.

AI.tldr: Pegasus is a low-resource framework that bridges the embodiment gap between human videos and robot learning by translating human demonstrations into robot-learnable data through graph-based intermediate representations and hierarchical affordance latent spaces, eliminating the need for raw video prompts.
AI.motivation: The key bottleneck in embodied AI is data scarcity for robots; while abundant human manipulation videos exist, robots cannot directly learn from them due to the embodiment gap between human morphology and robot hardware.
AI.method: Pegasus constructs a graph-based intermediate representation pipeline: Task Graph from human videos → Affordance and Constraint Graphs → Robot Planning Graph for robot-conditioned video generation. It uses a hierarchical affordance latent space to model object states, affordances, and tasks, and a closed-loop physics verifier to filter invalid generations based on kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits.
AI.result: Evaluated on GTEA Gaze+ and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 across diverse robot embodiments, Pegasus demonstrates reliable cross-embodiment translation on metrics including Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability.
AI.conclusion: Robot data generation can be reframed from a hardware collection problem into a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem, overcoming the embodiment gap without relying on raw video prompts.

title: FAS-R1: A Unified Multi-Task MLLM for Reasoning Face Anti-Spoofing
summary: Face anti-spoofing (FAS) is increasingly expected to provide not only bona fide/spoof decisions, but also attack semantics and image-grounded evidence for human inspection. Existing discriminative FAS models remain largely label-centric, while recent MLLM-based methods offer structured outputs but still rely mainly on supervised fine-tuning, often producing template-like rationales and weak optimization for difficult attacks. We propose FAS-R1, a two-stage reasoning-oriented MLLM framework for unified FAS prediction, covering authenticity classification, attack-type recognition and spoof-region localization.
