AI.motivation: To study the distinction between pricing accuracy and density recovery accuracy in option markets, addressing the overlooked fact that low pricing error does not imply correct latent density estimation.
AI.method: Two complementary benchmarks: (1) a controlled synthetic benchmark with known simulator-truth densities, (2) a chronological NIFTY benchmark for out-of-sample market prices. Compare a two-component lognormal mixture against learned operators (DeepONet, quote transformer) via multiple error metrics (L^1, Wasserstein, variance, quantile). Include numerical conditioning analysis and test-time adaptation.
AI.result: Lognormal mixture achieves lowest aggregate errors across metrics on synthetic data. DeepONet reduces 1% quantile error by 39.0% and variance error by 34.6% vs mixture; quote transformer reduces L^1 by 16.4% on misspecified Merton family. 95/126 pricing directions are numerically null; two densities with L^1=0.061 yield identical prices. On NIFTY data, test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but mixture/SVI fits remain far more accurate.
AI.conclusion: No universal winner exists; the optimal method depends on the target quantity and data regime. Inductive bias should be matched to the specific task (pricing vs. density recovery, in-distribution vs. misspecified).

title: HumanCLAW: Can Vision-Language Models Act Through a Body?
summary: Evaluating whether a vision-language model (VLM) can act through a physical body is challenging. The outcome of an action couples the VLM's decision with motor control. When a task fails, it is hard to tell whether the VLM made a bad choice or the motor controller simply failed to execute it, e.g., losing balance and falling. In this work, we introduce HumanCLAW, an evaluation framework that decouples action decision-making from low-level execution. At every step, a harnessed, off-the-shelf VLM issues an atomic skill command, and the command is translated into a sub-second chunk of continuous full-body motion with real physical consequences, including gravity and collisions. The body can therefore act freely in the physical world, while execution-side disturbances, balance and motor errors, are factored out. What remains measurable is the model's action intelligence: its moment-to-moment choice of what the body should execute next. Based on this framework, we build HumanCLAW-Bench: 1,218 long-horizon, egocentric find-navigate-interact episodes across 41 indoor scenes. We test nine state-of-the-art VLMs and find that none solves the benchmark; the best model reaches only a 16.8% success rate. Recognizing the target is not the bottleneck. What current VLMs lack is embodied self-awareness: they lose track of their own body, failing to tell where it is, whether it has reached the goal, or whether it has hit an obstacle.

AI.tldr: HumanCLAW is an evaluation framework that decouples VLM action decision-making from motor execution, enabling measurement of pure action intelligence. Testing nine state-of-the-art VLMs across 1,218 episodes, the best achieves only 16.8% success, revealing that VLMs lack embodied self-awareness (tracking body position, goal attainment, obstacle collision) rather than recognition ability.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations conflate VLM decision-making with motor control failures, making it impossible to determine whether task failures stem from bad decisions or poor execution (e.g., losing balance). A decoupled assessment of pure action intelligence is needed.
AI.method: HumanCLAW uses a harnessed VLM that issues atomic skill commands, which are translated into sub-second continuous full-body motion with real physics (gravity, collisions). This decouples high-level decisions from low-level execution, isolating the model's action intelligence for measurement.
AI.result: Nine state-of-the-art VLMs were tested on HumanCLAW-Bench (1,218 long-horizon episodes across 41 indoor scenes). The best model achieved only 16.8% success rate, and target recognition was not the limiting factor.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs fundamentally lack embodied self-awareness—they cannot track their own body's state (position, goal attainment, obstacle collisions)—which is the primary bottleneck for physical action intelligence, not visual recognition.

title: From Classification to Regression: Using a Fruitfly to Solve Equations
summary: We present a novel approach to regression tasks using classification which is motivated by the mechanism used by fruitflies to sense their environment. Specifically, we formulate a general framework for learning nonlinear input-output relationships by replacing complex global surrogate models with a finite library of representative local patterns. Since scientific data often occupy limited and recurring regions of the input space, we generate predictions by measuring similarities between a query and stored patterns, then combining their associated responses through weighted reconstruction. We apply this approach to nonlinear dynamical systems, data-driven regression, and physics-informed learning using suitable embeddings and similarity measures. For dynamical systems, our offline-online workflow extracts patterns from data or governing equations during the offline phase, while online prediction requires only similarity evaluation and response aggregation. This structure helps us reduce computational and memory demands while providing explicit control over the trade-off among accuracy, storage, and inference cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a classification-based regression framework inspired by fruitfly olfactory sensing, which uses a library of local patterns to approximate nonlinear input-output relationships, reducing computational cost while offering explicit control over accuracy-storage-inference trade-offs.
AI.motivation: To develop a computationally efficient regression framework that avoids complex global surrogate models by leveraging local pattern matching, inspired by biological sensing mechanisms in fruitflies.
AI.method: A framework that replaces global surrogate models with a finite library of representative local patterns; predictions are made by measuring similarities between queries and stored patterns, then combining responses via weighted reconstruction. An offline-online workflow extracts patterns from data or governing equations offline, while online inference only requires similarity evaluation and response aggregation.
AI.result: The approach reduces computational and memory demands while providing explicit control over the trade-off among accuracy, storage, and inference cost. It is applied successfully to nonlinear dynamical systems, data-driven regression, and physics-informed learning.
AI.conclusion: The fruitfly-inspired pattern-based regression offers an efficient alternative to global surrogate modeling, with practical benefits for scientific computing tasks including dynamical systems and physics-informed learning, particularly where data occupy limited and recurring regions of the input space.

title: VidMap: Exploiting Temporal Structure for Video-Based Structure-from-Motion
summary: Accurately recovering the camera's calibration and metric poses for any unconstrained video would unlock large-scale training data for navigation and scene understanding. The dominant approaches to this problem are severely limited: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is sensitive to initialization and transient failures due to its causal, incremental nature; it is often over-optimized for real-time operation and generally requires known camera calibration; while Structure-from-Motion (SfM) typically forgoes any image ordering, enabling optimal initialization and global optimization, but lacks robustness to visual symmetries and extreme motions. To bridge this gap, we introduce a system that combines the strong sequential constraints of SLAM with the flexibility and global optimization of offline SfM, enabling the metric reconstruction of arbitrary, long, uncalibrated videos. This system leverages recent advances in wide-baseline dense image matching, treats temporal ordering as a first-class citizen for reliable loop closure, and augments global optimization with metric monocular depth priors. As a result, thorough evaluations on diverse, challenging datasets that exhibit extreme motion and visual symmetries reveal that our approach is significantly more robust and accurate than both state-of-the-art SLAM and SfM, classical or learned, with given or unknown camera calibration. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cvg/vidmap.

AI.tldr: VidMap combines SLAM's sequential constraints with SfM's global optimization to enable robust metric reconstruction of arbitrary, long, uncalibrated videos, outperforming both SLAM and SfM on challenging datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches (SLAM and SfM) have complementary limitations: SLAM is sensitive to initialization and transient failures, requires known calibration, and is over-optimized for real-time operation; SfM lacks robustness to visual symmetries and extreme motions. The goal is to bridge this gap for accurate metric reconstruction from unconstrained videos.
AI.method: The system integrates sequential constraints from SLAM with the flexibility and global optimization of offline SfM, leverages wide-baseline dense image matching, treats temporal ordering as a first-class citizen for reliable loop closure, and augments global optimization with metric monocular depth priors.
AI.result: On diverse challenging datasets with extreme motion and visual symmetries, the approach is significantly more robust and accurate than both state-of-the-art SLAM and SfM (classical or learned), with either given or unknown camera calibration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system effectively bridges SLAM and SfM paradigms, enabling robust metric reconstruction from uncalibrated videos, with code publicly available.

title: Do You Really Need to Pretrain Q-Functions for Online RL Fine-Tuning?
summary: Pre-training followed by fine-tuning has become the dominant recipe for learning performant policies, and in value-based reinforcement learning (RL) this raises a natural question: given a pretrained policy, should the Q-function be pretrained on offline data too? Conventional wisdom suggests it should, but recent results show that online RL with a randomly-initialized Q-function can result in highly performant and reliable policies without needing to pretrain the Q-function. In this paper, we systematically study whether pretraining the Q-function actually helps when fine-tuning on top of a pretrained base policy. We find, surprisingly, that naive Q-function pretraining often provides little benefit over random initialization. We show this stems from a fundamental mismatch: the Q-function learned during pretraining targets the pretrained policy's Q-function, not the Q-function that online fine-tuning converges to, and this gap persists even after offline value maximization. Motivated by this finding, we propose Initialization via Policy Ensemble (IPE), a simple method that trains multiple diverse policies and uses their pooled rollouts to bootstrap the Q-function learning in online RL. Across a suite of challenging continuous control benchmarks, IPE yields an average 1.26x improvement in fine-tuning performance over naive Q-function pre-training.

AI.tldr: Systematic study showing naive Q-function pretraining offers little benefit over random initialization in value-based RL fine-tuning due to a mismatch between the pretrained Q-function (targeting the pretrained policy) and the Q-function online fine-tuning converges to; proposes IPE (Initialization via Policy Ensemble) that trains diverse policies and uses pooled rollouts to bootstrap Q-learning, achieving 1.26x improvement.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate whether pretraining the Q-function actually helps when fine-tuning on top of a pretrained base policy in value-based RL, given the conventional wisdom suggests it should but recent results show online RL with randomly-initialized Q-functions can be highly performant.
AI.method: Systematic study comparing naive Q-function pretraining vs random initialization; identification of fundamental mismatch between pretrained Q-function (targets pretrained policy) and online fine-tuning target; proposal of Initialization via Policy Ensemble (IPE) which trains multiple diverse policies and uses their pooled rollouts to bootstrap Q-function learning.
AI.result: Naive Q-function pretraining often provides little benefit over random initialization due to a persistent mismatch gap. IPE yields an average 1.26x improvement in fine-tuning performance across challenging continuous control benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The mismatch between pretrained Q-function objectives and online fine-tuning targets limits the benefit of naive Q-function pretraining; IPE effectively addresses this by leveraging diverse policy ensembles to bootstrap Q-learning.

title: TurboVLA: Real-Time Vision-Language-Action Model at 32 Hz on an RTX 4090 with <1 GB VRAM
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models commonly adopt an LLM-centric $V \to L \to A$ pathway, where visual observations are projected into the representation space of a large language model before being decoded into robot actions. Although effective, this design incurs substantial computation and memory overhead at every policy invocation. In this work, we introduce TurboVLA, a new VLA paradigm that reformulates the conventional $V \to L \to A$ pathway as a direct $V + L \to A$ mapping. Instead of using a large language model as the central interface between perception and action, TurboVLA independently encodes visual observations and language instructions, directly exchanges information between them through lightweight bidirectional vision-language interaction, and predicts continuous action chunks with a compact decoder. This simple design constructs task-conditioned representations directly from visual and linguistic features, significantly reducing the computational and memory costs of VLA inference. On LIBERO, TurboVLA achieves 97.7% average success with only 0.2B parameters, 31.2 ms inference latency, and 0.9 GB inference VRAM on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, matching or outperforming substantially larger VLA policies. These results establish TurboVLA as a simple and effective alternative to the prevailing LLM-centric VLA paradigm, offering a new perspective on how vision, language, and action can be connected for efficient robotic manipulation. Code is available at https://github.com/H-EmbodVis/TurboVLA.

AI.tldr: TurboVLA replaces the conventional LLM-centric V→L→A paradigm in vision-language-action models with a direct V+L→A mapping, using lightweight bidirectional vision-language interaction and a compact decoder to achieve 97.7% success on LIBERO with only 0.2B parameters, 31.2 ms latency, and 0.9 GB VRAM on an RTX 4090.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models adopt an LLM-centric V→L→A pathway that projects visual observations into LLM representation space before decoding actions, incurring substantial computational and memory overhead at every policy invocation.
AI.method: TurboVLA independently encodes visual observations and language instructions, exchanges information through lightweight bidirectional vision-language interaction, and predicts continuous action chunks using a compact decoder, formulating a direct V+L→A mapping without relying on a large language model as the central interface.
AI.result: On LIBERO, TurboVLA achieves 97.7% average success rate with only 0.2B parameters, 31.2 ms inference latency, and 0.9 GB inference VRAM on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, matching or outperforming substantially larger VLA policies.
AI.conclusion: TurboVLA establishes a simple and effective alternative to the LLM-centric VLA paradigm, offering a new perspective on connecting vision, language, and action for efficient robotic manipulation.
